#137660. ‘Get Out of the F—ing Tree!’ The Police Raided Our Deer Hunt

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

‘Get Out of the F—ing Tree!’ The Police Raided Our Deer Hunt

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that WHAT STARTED as a normal morning in the deer woods turned out to be the scariest day of my life.
  • Our state has an extended urban antlerless season that ends in late March, and this particular hunt occurred right after the state of Virginia revealed the “Stay at Home” order during the early Covid-19 pandemic.
  • Sources indicate that we were hunting in a neighborhood of multimillion-dollar homes on three- to five-acre lots, and the property we were on that day was a double lot of 10 acres total.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that WHAT STARTED as a normal morning in the deer woods turned out to be the scariest day of my life. It was March 2020, and my friend Billy Phillips and I were hunting one of the suburban properties we have permission on in northern Virginia.

Our state has an extended urban antlerless season that ends in late March, and this particular hunt occurred right after the state of Virginia revealed the “Stay at Home” order during the early Covid-19 pandemic. That particular order allowed you to leave home for a couple of reasons, and hunting was one of them.

Sources indicate that we were hunting in a neighborhood of multimillion-dollar homes on three- to five-acre lots, and the property we were on that day was a double lot of 10 acres total. In our world, that’s humongous.

We parked at the end of an old driveway and walked a short way to our hunting spots. We climbed into our trees to set up about 100 yards from each other, with Billy closer to the trucks than my stand. Then, just as daylight broke, I spotted the lights of a car near where we parked. I looked through my binos and saw that an older Ford Taurus had pulled up. I remember thinking, Oh, this is kind of odd.

It has been revealed that I texted Billy. “Can you see the cars?”.

“Yeah, I’m looking at them,” he texted back.

Then I saw Billy’s truck bed light turn on.

“He’s in my car,” Billy texted again. “I’m getting down.”.

Industry observers note that at this point the sun was fully up and we could clearly see our surroundings. As Billy descended his tree, I saw a police officer in full uniform coming down the little hill toward us with an M4 in his hands. I pulled out my phone to record footage, the kind of video that says, Look at the unusual things we deal with while hunting in the suburbs.

Then I realized the cop had his weapon shouldered and was pointing it at Billy. He was screaming at him.

It has been revealed that “Get on the ground! Get on the fucking ground!”.

What he was saying was concerning, but the tension in the officer’s voice was worse. Billy was packing up his sticks as the cop approached. If Billy had turned around while holding the sticks or if he still had his crossbow in his hands, I don’t even want to think about what might have happened.

“Where’s your buddy?” the cop started yelling, getting even more aggressive. “Where’s your buddy?”.

And I’m like, “Sir, I’m over here.”.

“Get out of the fucking tree,” he yelled.

“OK,” I replied, “it’s going to take me a minute.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I didn’t ask for feedback. I told you to get down here.”.

In a recent development, the cop screamed at both of us the whole time it took me to get down. When I walked up to the cop, he spoke into his radio.

“You can take the guns off them now.”.

We were obviously perplexed, and he explained that he had snipers in the woods with their rifles trained on us.

“What is going on here?” I asked. “What is happening?”.

“Shut up,” he told me. “I’m asking questions here. Hands on your head and turn around.”.

I kept persisting with questions, trying to figure out why we were being searched at gunpoint and who this police officer was. The man wouldn’t tell us anything and proceeded to pat us down.

In a recent development, “I’m not a regular cop,” was all he said. “I’m a special cop.”.

Read Next: The Best Tree Saddles, Tested and Reviewed.

According to recent reports, when the officer asked us what we were doing at this property, we explained that we are deer hunters and that we had permission to be here. I pulled up the signed permission slip from the landowner and showed it to him. Then I asked again what he was doing here. The officer told us that they spotted us on a UAV — an unmanned aerial vehicle. He was suggesting he had a military drone 30,000 feet above us, which is completely ridiculous for our county or most any police department.

“This is Fairfax County,” I noted. “What are you talking about?”.

His demeanor shifted and he got less aggressive — especially when I asked him why he was going through our vehicles.

According to recent reports, “You had a wire on the floor, and I thought it was a bomb,” he said to Billy. Billy explained that he works in landscaping, and that he has sprinkler-head components in his truck.

According to recent reports, by now we were starting to get nervous, and I noticed the officer’s uniform didn’t look quite right. There was something off about him. We kept asking why he was searching our cars without cause, and why he was on private property.

He didn’t give us his card or an explanation, and no other officers indicated up. After the adrenaline of having a gun pointed at us wore off, Billy and I ran through what had just happened.

Sources indicate that I told Billy that I thought the guy must be impersonating law enforcement, because the whole interaction just didn’t sit right with me. Billy and I mentor several police officers who are learning to hunt, and we’re huge supporters of police in general. Mind you, this was when Covid lockdowns were at their peak, and there was mass civil unrest throughout the country. The last thing we wanted to do was blast the police.

Recent findings suggest that still, we needed answers. We sent the short video clip I had recorded to a few of our police officer buddies, and one called me right away. He explained that it didn’t look right, and that what happened is not standard police procedure. He asked where we were and made a few phone calls to see if he could find out any details for us.

When my buddy called me back, he was laughing so hard he could barely speak. The man who had just ordered us down from our trees at gunpoint was indeed a police officer known as the department’s Tackleberry. (In the Police Academy movies, Tackleberry is a tryhard who’s overzealous in his enforcement.) This particular police officer had been on desk duty and was sent out on patrol as a result of scheduling issues caused by Covid.

My buddy learned that the officer had gotten turned around, thought he was at a park, and that we were doing something illegal. Billy and I had a meeting with the guy’s captain, who apologized profusely. We decided to leave it at that.

It was a terrifying and confusing ordeal while it was happening, but now that a few years have passed, it’s just another crazy story from our time hunting the D.C. suburbs. Here’s this guy who thought he was busting the biggest crime ring of all time and instead ended up nearly arresting a couple rednecks in camo.

This story first ran on March 17, 2023.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Black Diamond Distance Carbon Z FKT Trekking Poles.

Janji Rainrunner Pack Jacket 2.0.

Garmin Fenix 8 Pro AMOLED Sapphire.

Smartwool Performance Run Targeted Cushion Glow Track Crew Socks.

Industry observers note that love it or hate it, the holiday season is apparently here. Sure, that means it’s time to panic-shop for gifts. But as trail runners, it’s also a once-in-a-year opportunity to score the biggest deals on the gear we need. (Yes, need.) That’s why I spent way too long pouring through REI’s Holiday Sale to find the best deals on the trail running shoes, apparel, and accoutrement that is genuinely used and loved by me and the Trail Runner team.

From November 13-23, REI is running its biggest sale of the season. Also during this window REI members get 20% off one full-price item—such as the Salomon Adv Skin 12 Hydration Vest, aka my favorite hydration vest. REI members also get another 20% off one item at REI.com/outlet. (Use the code Holiday2026 for both.).

Below, you’ll find my hand-picked items from the thousands on site. You can also go wild and check out the full sale for yourself.

In my humble opinion the Black Diamond Distance Carbon Z FKT Trekking Poles are hands-down the best trekking poles on the market. That’s thanks to the ingenious glove strap system that affixes to the pole with a magnet—no more faffing around trying to get your poles on and off with two hands. The gloves themselves provide excellent energy transfer, and the carbon poles are super light but also plenty sturdy. I used them for full 110-mile a lap of Mount Blanc this summer and they still look and feel as good as new.

In a recent development, it’s a tried and true staple for a reason. My footwork has never felt more precise than when I’m wearing the La Sportiva Bushido. That’s thanks to a specially-designed midsole that hugs your foot, Ghillie lacing, and an ultra grippy outsole. The III has an extra breathable upper and side panels that increase airflow but keep the rocks out. If you’re running on a lot of technical trails, this shoe is hard to beat.

Industry observers note that are they for hiking? For fashion? Why not both! The Keen Jasper Zionic Sneakers came on my radar when Harry Styles and Zoe Kravitz were spotted hoofing it around Latest York City in matching pairs. I, too, am now a proud owner of a pair and they nail the combination of comfort and style. I would most certainly wear them on a hike, and I also wore them to a wedding rehearsal dinner. (Got multiple compliments.).

Most of the time, the only thing standing between nasty winter rain and a good time is quality rain gear. That’s why this Janji raincoat is on my wishlist. I’ve never tested an item from Janji that I didn’t love; the Janji Aurora Fleece Tight and Atlas Multi Pant got my legs (and soul) through winter last year. With 2.5 layers of waterproof yet breathable laminate and fully taped seams, the Janji Rainrunner Pack Jacket looks up for the task. But what’s really catching my eye is the venting around the torso—no point in staying dry if you’re going to get super sweaty. Plus, it’s just a pretty sleek looking jacket.

It’s cute, it’s functional, and it comes in tons of both subtle and fun colors. I love the Janji Groundwork Longbra for warm runs, gym time, and even everyday wear. Plus, there’s a pocket in the back that’s massive enough to hold a smart phone—if your shoulders are flexible enough to reach it. (Sadly mine are not … probably need to take this tank to a yoga class.).

I have worn the women’s version of the Mountain Hardwear Jor Alloy Tights and can attest they keep your legs warm and free on the coldest winter runs. That’s thanks to strategically-placed fleece where you want to stay warm and stretch where you want to move. The waistband is, crucially, very comfortable and fully adjustable thanks to the drawstring.

Sources indicate that whether you’re running, ski mountaineering, or curling up on the couch, sometimes you just want to be cozy. The Mountain Hardwear Summit Grid Major Grid Hoody, while a mouthful to say, is the answer during those times. A cinch around the hood and the waist makes it practical for cold outings. (The hood actually stays up! Cold air doesn’t fly up your torso!) And that kangaroo pocket is just begging to keep your hands warm.

Recent findings suggest that once you switch to wool, you can’t go back. And this merino wool base layer is la crème de la crème. The Icebreaker Merino 200 Oasis Long-Sleeve Crewe Thermal Top is sturdy but soft, warm but breathable, doesn’t stink, has a UPF of 20, and transitions beautifully from the trails to daily life.

For trail runners, there is one watch to rule them all. And it’s the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro. With built-in InReach tech, it’s a fully-functioning SOS device—no phone required. Send messages and get location check-ins without cell service, reach the Garmin Response coordination center for 24/7 help, and let friends and family know where you are with location sharing. And of course, it’s got all the bells and whistles of a top-tier GPS watch, including 78 hours of battery life in GPS mode. Plus with an AMOLED Sapphire face it’s basically indestructible. If you’ve been eyeing this bad boy now is the time to send it.

I live in these Smartwool Performance socks during winter, both on the run and in daily life. That’s because they are super warm but also pretty thin. In other words, I can wear my normal shoe size without squeezing my toes. Bonus points for fun patterns.

I’ve been using an older version of this pillow for years and can confidently say whether you’re fastpacking or simply want to sleep better when you’re traveling, this Sea to Summit Aeros Premium Pillow will revolutionize your life. While it’s inflatable and weighs next to nothing (3.5 oz for the regular size), it’s got a memory foam topper that will fool you otherwise. (Pssst, it would also make an excellent gift!).

Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

In a recent development, with all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the big ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.).

Recent findings suggest that some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

In a recent development, however, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

According to recent reports, it’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

According to recent reports, unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

According to recent reports, beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern Latest Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Recent findings suggest that hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Significant Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

Industry observers note that spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Big Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the Newly introduced Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Industry observers note that crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Recent findings suggest that why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Industry observers note that perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

Winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

Desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

On long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries quickly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

Recent findings suggest that my favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

#137621. I Hunted Ducks and Geese During the Glory Days of Earthquake Lake

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2889 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

I Hunted Ducks and Geese During the Glory Days of Earthquake Lake

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was a good day for waterfowl hunters.
  • According to recent reports, I slid the overhead hatch back and stuck my head up and out of the blind.
  • In a recent development, the blind was one of the biggest I had ever seen, and it was also almost invisible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was a good day for waterfowl hunters. Wisps of fog seeped out of the melting landscape, and the sky was so low and solid that the geese—if they came—would be close to the deck. And it was cold. Two days before, a savage cold wave had swept across Tennessee, plastering trees and highways with ice and freezing ponds thicker than anyone could remember. Ducks and geese had been sitting it out, but on this third day, the ice was melting, and they would fly.

According to recent reports, I slid the overhead hatch back and stuck my head up and out of the blind. Earlier it had been too dark to see how we were situated. I found that we were in a soybean field of perhaps 300 acres, already plowed for the spring planting. There was sparse timber on all sides. To the south, the way hunters faced when standing in the blind, the timber was not so tall or thick, but there was the heavy undergrowth that grows at water’s edge. The lake is closer than I thought, I mentioned to myself. It’s only 100 yards or so away.

In a recent development, the blind was one of the biggest I had ever seen, and it was also almost invisible. From a duck’s overhead view, it no doubt looked like a rush-covered finger of land surrounded on three sides by timber, water, and waterfowl decoys—hundreds of them.

According to recent reports, thus oriented, I closed the camouflaged hatch and placed my feet near the gas heater. Sheer luxury! Being there almost made up for all those miserable days I have spent crouched in freezing mud holes. Perhaps a time or two before, in Texas and Louisiana, I’d been in more luxurious shooting stands, but they were small houses built on stilts above the water. This was a blind dug into the ground, lined with concrete, and covered with earth that had been planted with suitable cover. The blind’s eyes on the outside world were 12 sliding hatches.

According to recent reports, inside, the padded theater seats were as comfy as easychairs. Theater seats! I thought. Who in hell would have thought of putting theater seats in a duck blind? But it was perfect! The spring-loaded bottoms snapped up out of the way when you rose to shoot. That gave a man more foot and leg room and eliminated bruised shins if he turned around for backyard shots. I’m forever scraping my shins on the sharp-edged board benches found in most blinds.

Sources indicate that as the light increased, so did the yipping of the Canada geese rafted up on Lake Isom just beyond the brushy boundary. A few minutes before, the even din of honking had changed pitch when a raft of Canadas took wing. Moments later another flight heaved into the morning fog.

Our lookout Jerry Jones made no sign that geese were coming our way, but the atmosphere inside the blind was becoming so charged with excitement that you could almost touch it. Feet shuffled, experienced hunters quaked with anticipation, and hands rattled shotshells in jacket pockets to make sure fast reloads were ready. Overhead and close by, there was a whistle of teal. Jerry’s eyes followed their crossing flight, but he did not signal us to shoot, because he didn’t want to spoil our chances for the major honkers that could be only minutes away.

From the lake came another din of geese taking off, and Jerry pulled his head lower and tightened his grip on his Browning autoloading magnum. Then he crouched even lower, eyes level with his lookout hole, and stated, “They’re ours boys. Get ready—now!”.

Shotgun barrels poked out of the blind, and there was ragged fire at eight or nine geese that were angling by to our left. The closest bird went limp in midair, but the one I fired at twice merely did the double wobble of a wise old goose that knows he’s being shot at.

Industry observers note that long ago I learned that in each flight of waterfowl there are one or two obvious birds. They are closer or bigger or out in front, and they tend to draw fire. When I’m sharing a blind with other hunters, I therefore pass up the obvious targets and go for a more obscure member of the flight. That bird is all mine, and I know for sure if I hit or miss. This time the obvious bird did draw most of the fire and was the only one to fall. Happily there was no chorus of “I got him!” that sometimes mars such events. These men, most of whom I’d met only that morning, were too experienced and too polite for that. Instead, each one claimed to have missed by several feet and that the goose must have been felled by the youngest member of the party, 15-year-old Charlie Lawrence.

In a recent development, “I did?” he whooped in wide-eyed amazement. “And that means you’ll have to fetch it,” Charlie’s father almost managed to say before the young hunter was out of the blind and sprinting after the prize, his rubber boots going flub-flub and launching dollops of river-bottom mud from the Mississippi in all directions.

Whoever first remarked that you can tell a lot about a man’s character by hunting with him really knew what he was talking about. Settling back into my posh seat, I knew I had learned a lot about my new acquaintances already and had a feeling that we would all be good friends before the day ended.

The only one of us who hadn’t pulled a trigger on the geese was Ralph McDonald, the well-known wildlife artist. His sliding hatch had stuck when the action started, so he had to sit out the first round. But Jerry Jones fixes that in a hurry by leaving the hatch open and covering the opening with a layer of cane that could easily be pushed aside. I liked that arrangement better than moving the hatch, so he fixed me up the same way. It gave me a better look at incoming birds.

In addition to Jerry, Ralph, and myself, our shooting party included H. Lea Lawrence, his teen-aged sons David and Charlie, country-music star Jim Ed Brown, plus Bill Morrison and Tom Callery. Lea, who lives in Nashville, is an outdoor writer whose name is familiar to readers of OUTDOOR LIFE. Morrison and Callery are field and legislative assistants to U.S. Senator William Brock of Tennessee. When I met Morrison and Callery that morning and learned of their political connections, I made a mental note to bend their ears about pending firearms legislation.

But there was no time for that now—ducks were coming, and Jerry was making seductive sounds on his big-barreled duck call. I couldn’t see the incomers from my angle, but it was easy enough to pinpoint their position by watching Jerry’s eyes. As they came closer, he crouched lower in the blind, and I knew they were within range even before he whisper-shouted, “Now!”.

In a recent development, about 10 spoonbills were winging low and fast from right to left in front of the blind. I swung my 12-gauge double, a Model 21 Winchester, through one of the trailers, but before I could press the trigger the bird’s head kicked back and he collapsed in midair. Then I was aware of three or four other ducks tumbling out of the formation, but my attention was concentrated on another spoonbill. I swung the barrels ahead by about two feet and pressed the trigger. The load of No. 4s folded the spoonbill so cleanly that there was no need to think about a follow-up shot, so I chased the barrels to the next closest bird and gave him the remaining round. It was a straightaway shot, and the range was rapidly increasing with each beat of his wings. For a moment it looked like a miss, but then the spoonbill did a turnover and went into a power dive before thumping hard on the semifrozen field. At 60 yards, perhaps more, it had been a lucky shot, but all eyes had been on me, and the welfare of my ego was at stake.

Recent findings suggest that while David and Charlie fetched the downed waterfowl, I made the innocent mistake of asking Ralph if he had scored on the spoonbills. Though he is a leading wildlife artist whose paintings have twice been featured on the cover of the Ducks Unlimited magazine, he has a well-earned reputation as a hard-luck waterfowl hunter. On his goose hunts something always goes wrong, and he was still looking to shoot his first honker.

Jerry, who owns and operates Sunset Court and Dock on Reelfoot Lake, is one of those old-fashioned guides who believes that a day not spent hunting or fishing is a day wasted. Just to make sure that he and his customers get in plenty of both, his fees for a guided goose-and-duck hunt—including lodging, a heated blind, decoys, transport to the blind, plus some of the finest duck calling and yarn spinning you’re likely to hear anywhere—are no more than you’d expect to pay to spend the night in a rundown Upcoming York hotel.

While I was hunting the Reelfoot and Lake Isom area, the local waterfowl population was estimated at some 70,000 geese and about a quarter of a million ducks, mainly gadwalls and mallards.

Historic Reelfoot Lake is well known among waterfowlers and it is an easy day’s drive from many large Midwestern and Eastern cities. Lake Isom, however, remains distinctly undiscovered, even though it is only a few miles away (see map, page 89).

In a recent development, hunting seasons run from December into January. The duck limit is based on the point system. Some ducks, such as pintails and spoonbills (shovelers), are rated at only 10 points each, so it is possible to bag 10 ducks plus two geese in a single day. That’s a lot of shooting.

In a recent development, ralph was about halfway through a lengthy explanation of how he had failed to get off a single shot at the geese when Jerry shouted “Get down!” at the two young Lawrence brothers, who were still gathering ducks. Another flight of spoonbills had just cleared Isom’s boundary and were coming directly at us. Charlie had left his shotgun in the blind, but older and wiser David had his pump ready and neatly dropped a drake.

Recent findings suggest that the first half-hour had produced a goose and a half a dozen ducks—rich promise of a good day of shooting—but by midmorning the action tapered off to only an occasional shot at a passing duck. For some reason known only to themselves, the geese had decided to leave by the western side of the lake. We could hear their comings and goings, but none came within half a mile. Over a breakfast of ham and eggs cooked in a subterranean kitchen attached to the blind and complete with gas stove, we discussed the sagging action. Jerry allowed that we could move to a blind closer to the flyway the honkers had selected that day. Jerry owns or has access to 15 blinds.

Recent findings suggest that after a quick scouting sortie, he asked for volunteers to try another blind situated where the honkers seemed to be heading, but he also told us the road was bad and we’d have to walk a ways. Jim Ed Brown, Lea Lawrence, and I volunteered, but not without some misgivings on my part.

Ralph McDonald elected to stay where he was, because, as he put it, he’d “… had a vision that the geese would soon come that way.”.

Even before we got to our fresh blind, there was no doubt that Jerry was right. While walking about a quarter of a mile through a sparse stand of scrub timber, we spotted three flights of geese skimming low over a field of winter wheat. They landed almost in the new blind.

Industry observers note that “Holy catfish!” said Jim Ed in the soft Southern accents that have made him a favorite of Grand Ole Opry fans. “All I need is two.”.

According to recent reports, just then six or eight more honkers slipped in low over the wheatfield, wings cupped to land. Before they touched down, the leader thought better of it, and they flared hard left, leveled off treetop high, and headed straight at us. We were almost through the scrub brush by then, and there wasn’t much cover, but we ducked into what concealment there was.

It has been revealed that “Get ready,” Jerry whispered just an arm’s length to my left. Like me, he was half hidden in a honeysuckle bank. Just then Jim Ed and Lea opened up, and two honkers dropped at once. A third, hit hard, scaled overhead, and Jerry or me, or both of us, hit him at less than 30 yards and folded him cleanly.

The rest of the formation had swerved violently when Lea and Jim Ed started shooting, and they were out of range before I could come to bear with my second barrel. The geese were still reasonably close to Jim Ed, and with the last shot in his Model 12 Winchester pump, another Canada pitched down, wing feathers humming in the rush of the fall.

“Friends,” drawled Jim Ed, “this is what I was brought up to call good goose hunting. I’ve got my limit, and we ain’t even in the blind.”.

The timing was perfect, because less than an hour later Jim Ed was scheduled to leave by charter plane to tape his popular “Nashville On The Road” TV show. So he and Jerry took the four honkers back to the truck while Lea and I went on to the blind. Jerry got back as quickly as he could.

Sources indicate that we had no more than settled ourselves when a flight of perhaps 20 geese came soaring up the field. Jerry called, and they began to circle. When we stood to fire, they flared sharply and momentarily gave us that near-motionless target goose hunters love. I shot at a bird on the far right end of the formation so there would be little chance that Lea and I would double on the same target. The Canada spun and fell without a flutter.

Meanwhile Lea was doing the same with a honker he had cut out of the flight.

That evening we feasted on lake-country froglegs, catfish, hush puppies, and tart cole slaw. It had been a great day for everyone except Ralph McDonald.

“I was sure my hunch about those geese was a good one,” he lamented, pouring himself a stiff snort of Reelfoot tea, “but I never got a shot. My record is intact.”.

Read Next: I Gave Up My Duck Blind to Hunt Where the Mallards Actually Are.

It has been revealed that reelfoot Lake in far western Tennessee was formed by the Fresh Madrid earthquakes of 1811-12. The catastrophe depressed some 50,000 acres that were later submerged by water from the Mississippi River. The surge was so great that the Mississippi is said to have flowed backward for a while. Due to siltation, plant succession, and drainage, Reelfoot Lake now covers about 18,000 acres.

A colorful legend accounts for the lake’s name. A Chickasaw chief suffered from a deformed or club foot and reeled when he walked. Chief Reelfoot could not persuade any of the Chickasaw maidens to become his wife, so he and his warriors kidnapped a Choctaw maiden named Starlight. Her father, who would not allow the marriage because of Reelfoot’s deformity, was so angered that he ordered his medicine men to bring down a terrible vengeance on Reelfoot and his people. That, the legend has it, was the cause of the earthquake.

It has been revealed that lake Isom, scene of the waterfowl hunt in this story, was isolated from the substantial lake when a road was built around the southern end of the lake. A water-control structure and a ditch aided in draining the land that lies between the lakes today. The lake was given a name when the site was acquired for a waterfowl refuge from the Isom family.

Industry observers note that reelfoot’s excellent waterfowl habitat made it one of the most famous hunting areas on the Mississippi Flyway. The open-water portions attracted a variety of diving ducks, particularly canvasbacks. Mallards were most abundant and most popular among gunners. Eventually, however, the canvasbacks almost disappeared, and restrictive limits were imposed on mallard shooting. In the late 1960’s, with a one-mallard limit, Reelfoot had an all-time low in hunter usage.

It has been revealed that as the mallards and some other ducks increased in numbers after the low, and limits were increased, the popularity of Reelfoot Lake among gunners increased somewhat, but it is taking a while for hunters to realize that it’s the same hotspot. Reelfoot is as good today as it ever was, and Lake Isom is just as good. Neither Reelfoot nor Isom is managed by the state, but public hunting is permitted at Reelfoot. At Lake Isom the hunting is on private land.

Breaking: The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level.
  • Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain.
  • Recent findings suggest that behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Recent findings suggest that behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

In a recent development, located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

It has been revealed that posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

According to recent reports, when he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

Sources indicate that “My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”.

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

According to recent reports, “The rope would drop us off here,” he claims. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

It has been revealed that mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

It has been revealed that infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

According to recent reports, “Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

It has been revealed that mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

It has been revealed that by the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”.

Industry observers note that in a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

In a recent development, the chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

It has been revealed that “It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza notes. “The people remarked, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”.

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”.

According to recent reports, scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

According to recent reports, without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Recent findings suggest that glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

It has been revealed that since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he claims. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”.

Since the collapse of the glacier, a fresh group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he states. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I remarked, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”.

Sources indicate that inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque indicates, “but mountain sports have not.”.

It has been revealed that while private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque claims.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he indicates. “We have the potential.”.

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an important mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

In a recent development, for all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he says.

It has been revealed that through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he notes.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.

Review: Cumulus Mountlite Down Jacket

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sectionhiker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Cumulus Mountlite is a very warm ultralight winter down jacket designed for winter hiking, ski touring, and climbing.
  • The Mountlite’s key benefit is weight efficiency.
  • It has been revealed that to protect the down insulation from external moisture and wind, Cumulus utilizes 10D Pertex Quantum for the outer shell and liner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cumulus Mountlite is a very warm ultralight winter down jacket designed for winter hiking, ski touring, and climbing. Weighing just 12.9 ounces, it is insulated with 6.3 ounces of highly compressible 900-fill-power goose down, delivering an outstanding warmth-to-weight ratio. An adjustable hood, a #3 YKK zipper with dual sliders, and three zippered pockets round out this impressively warm jacket.

The Mountlite’s key benefit is weight efficiency. The jacket weighs 12.9 ounces in size medium, making it a lightweight option among dedicated winter layers. Of that total weight, 6.35 ounces is 900-fill-power Polish goose-down insulation. This high ratio means that roughly half the garment’s total mass is dedicated directly to trapping body heat. Premium down allows the jacket to compress efficiently and recover its loft promptly after being unpacked in cold environments.

It has been revealed that to protect the down insulation from external moisture and wind, Cumulus utilizes 10D Pertex Quantum for the outer shell and liner. This fabric provides a windproof barrier while allowing interior moisture vapor to escape during low-intensity movement. The fabric is thin to minimize total weight but requires careful handling around sharp winter tools.

The hood is shaped to offer close coverage around the face and neck, helping to retain heat during windy stops. The zipper features a standard YKK zipper with 2 sliders that operates reliably in freezing conditions. For draft management, the jacket uses low-profile elastic wrist cuffs and an adjustable hem cinch to seal out cold air from below. The external pockets, one chest and two handwarmer pockets, are positioned to remain accessible while wearing a backpack hip belt or a climbing harness. The jacket is stuffable in its left hand pocket and has an external loop.

The jacket’s insulation is held in sewn-through baffles, which you wouldn’t expect in a jacket this warm. This isn’t the most efficient design because the stitching creates small cold spots with little or no insulation. It may also provide less loft and warmth than a box-baffle jacket. Still, sewn-through construction can be lighter, which is why I suspect Cumulus used it here. I’m honestly amazed at how warm this jacket is regardless of the baffle construction technique, and it is a delight to carry on summit hikes because it packs up so small when compressed.

The Mountlite has an athletic cut, which you should keep in mind when sizing. Its adjustable hood (rear toggle) is helmet-compatible, a useful feature for ski touring, climbing, and mountaineering. Even so, it still insulates very well when used without a helmet. The hood can help reduce heat loss during exposed stops and windy conditions.

The Cumulus Mountlite is an exceptional winter layer for anyone who values serious warmth without accepting unnecessary weight or bulk. Its 900-fill-power goose down, lightweight Pertex Quantum shell, thoughtful hood design, harness-friendly pockets, and compact packed size make it remarkably capable on winter hikes, ski tours, climbs, and summit pushes. Despite its sewn-through construction and delicate shell fabric, the jacket delivers impressive warmth in a package that is easy to carry and quick to deploy when conditions turn cold.

Sources indicate that the Mountlite stands out as a highly refined piece of winter gear: exceptionally warm for its weight, versatile in the mountains, and small enough to keep in a pack on every outing. For cold-weather adventures where warmth, packability, and low weight matter most, it is an outstanding choice.

Disclosure: Cumulus donated a jacket for review.

Winter Bivy Sack Guide (2026)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sectionhiker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Winter bivy sacks were first developed as solo shelters for mountaineering and climbing where participants were interested in lightweight and highly compressible camping gear.
  • Winter bivy sacks are different from three-season bivy sacks, which are often used in conjunction with a tarp for insect and splashback protection, where rain hitting the ground can bounce back and wet your quilt or sleeping bag.
  • Recent findings suggest that the biggest advantage of a winter bivy sack is that you can use it anywhere you want to stop and sleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Winter bivy sacks were first developed as solo shelters for mountaineering and climbing where participants were interested in lightweight and highly compressible camping gear. Bivy Sacks are also an attractive option for backpacking hunters, backcountry skiers, and winter backpackers who want the lightest and smallest shelter they can carry for overnight or emergency use.

Winter bivy sacks are different from three-season bivy sacks, which are often used in conjunction with a tarp for insect and splashback protection, where rain hitting the ground can bounce back and wet your quilt or sleeping bag. In contrast, a winter bivy sack is intended as a standalone shelter or used with a snow shelter such as a trench or snow cave. Winter bivy sacks tend to be much higher in volume to hold winter-weight sleeping bags without compressing the insulation and work best in dry and cold conditions where precipitation is in the form of snow.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest advantage of a winter bivy sack is that you can use it anywhere you want to stop and sleep. Most models don’t require tent stakes or poles, and they pack down very small, which is great when you want to keep your winter gear lightweight and compact. Most winter bivy sacks use waterproof/breathable top fabrics to reduce internal condensation and waterproof base fabrics to keep your sleeping bag and pad dry. Insect netting is also available in some cold weather bivy sacks and can be useful when they’re used in spring conditions when bugs begin to emerge,.

Sources indicate that there are many advantages to sleeping in a waterproof bivy sack over a tent. It is easy to find a place to put a bivy sack at night since it only requires as much space as your sleeping pad and sleeping bag. Simply unroll your bivy sack, slip your sleeping pad and sleeping bag inside, and crawl in. This makes them suitable for sleeping on narrow mountain ledges or in forested glades where there’s just enough space to lie between two trees.

There are no tent stakes to freeze into the ground so you can get inside without delay and get warm. Being waterproof, you don’t have to lie on top of a groundsheet either, since the bottom of a waterproof bivy sack is designed to keep you dry. Bivy sacks also add a few degrees of insulation to your sleep system and make great emergency shelters for solo winter hikers, provided you carry a sleeping pad and enough insulation to get through the night.

In a recent development, bivy sacks are much more confining than tents, with only enough space for you and a few small personal items. You can’t really do anything inside one except listen to podcasts or go to sleep. It’s awkward to change out of your wet clothes or put on dry clothes inside, depending on the type of bivy sack you have; it can be damn hard to put on your boots, even to go for a pee at night. There’s no place to store your backpack, and the rest of your gear will be fully exposed at night without any cover.

Bivy sacks are also more prone to internal condensation than a tent, even when manufactured with waterproof breathable materials. You’re best off keeping them open or unzipped at night to reduce the temperature difference between the inside of the bivy and the outside, which causes condensation. Tent condensation occurs for the same reason, but tents have better ventilation and more volume, so it’s easier to keep your sleeping bag dry when it occurs.

Despite these disadvantages, I have friends who swear by their winter bivy sacks because they’re so fast to deploy compared to a tent or tarp. I’ve used winter bivy sacks and can appreciate their strengths, but winter nights last a very long time, and it’s nice to have a little extra space to change your clothes or sleep with your gear inside your tent. Whichever you choose depends on what you’re trying to accomplish.

There are three types of winter bivy sacks to choose from:.

In a recent development, there are two types of hooped bivy sacks: those with front entrances that you slide into feet first and those that you can enter from the side. Both come with one more short fiberglass or carbon fiber rods that give shape to the hood and prevent it from collapsing onto your head or torso.

It has been revealed that the head-end of a hooped front entrance bivy is usually screened with a solid cover that can be zippered closed for warmth or to block wind or rain. This design provides good ventilation for your head and helps to expel the water vapor in your breath. The Outdoor Research Helium UL Bivy is a good example of the front entry hooped design.

Side-entry hooped bivy sacks usually have a zipper along one side so you can easily get in and out of them. This design is also easier to vent because you can roll up the top cover in dry weather to reduce internal condensation. The Outdoor Research Alpine XT Bivy is a good example of a hooped bivy with a side entrance.

The simplest and lightest-weight winter bivy sacks are little more than sleeping bag covers. Some have drawstrings that you can pull closed over your head; some have shaped mummy-style hoods or simple slits above the face for ventilation. While not as livable or as well-ventilated as the hooped bivy sack designs described above, they do the job if you want a highly compressible, ultralight weather protection for your sleep system.

There are multiple features and trade-offs to consider when choosing a winter bivy sack.

Recent findings suggest that A waterproof/breathable top fabric is important for venting water vapor and reducing internal condensation that can make your sleeping bag wet. However, unlike rain jackets, most bivy sack manufacturers do not list the laboratory measurements used to rate waterproofing (hydrostatic head, abbreviated “HH”) or breathability (movable water transmission rate, abbreviated “MVTR”). That can make performance comparisons between different bivy sacks difficult.

Recent findings suggest that if headroom matters, consider a bivy shelter with a hooped design. These bivy sacks come with a flexible pole that slides into the hood to create more volume around your face and shoulders. The tradeoff is that they tend to be heavier than more minimal bivy sacks.

Winter bivy sacks tend to be high volume to fit bulky winter sleeping bags and inflatable pads with a high R-value. When choosing a bivy sack you want to ensure that there is enough room for your sleeping bag insulation to fully loft and that it’s not compressed by having too tight a fit.

Industry observers note that it’s much easier to get in and out of a bivy sack that has a zipper along the side than one that only has a “hatch” at the head end, to crawl in and out of. You’ll stay drier if the ground is covered in snow and it’s much easier to put on and take off your shoes.

If you blueprint to bivy in early spring when biting insects emerge, make sure to get a winter bivy sack with a mesh panel over the face so you can sleep without insects biting your face at night. If you only plan to sleep in a bivy sack in winter or in snow caves, a mesh panel will be less important. For warmer weather use, I’d encourage you to invest in an ultralight bivy sack or bug shelter rather than a winter bivy sack, since they’re much cooler to use. See our 10 Best Backpacking Bug Shelters for our recommended three-season bivy sacks.

According to recent reports, don’t forget to consider the weight of the bivy sack and its packed size, since one of the chief benefits of using a bivy sack is gear weight and size reduction. There’s often a tradeoff between features and weight/size, but some winter bivy sacks are surprisingly lightweight and compressible.

When in doubt, order a bivy sack (check the retailer’s return policy) and lie in it at home to see if it fits. This will probably tell you a lot more about whether it will work for you than comparing the specs of multiple models listed online. Check that you can fit your sleeping pad and sleeping bag inside, and that the footbox is large enough for your feet.

Recent findings suggest that there is a class of emergency bivy sacks that are only intended for emergency use such as the SOL Escape Lite Bivy. These are made with thin reflective aluminized fabric and lack the durability or breathability of the multiuse bivy sacks listed above.

Industry observers note that one summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

And then we were on top of each other.

Recent findings suggest that A grizzly cub, massive as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

“Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, substantial and fast and flat to the ground.

Sources indicate that I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

Excerpted from the novel Nearshore (Viking, 2026).

Palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo. It was a Whaler circling clockwise fast and tight, maybe a quarter mile beyond the surf.

He’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. But then he got the call about the boat, and now that he saw it spinning he also saw that his day was officially fucked. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

The wake’s widening spiral told him the wheel had been hard to starboard a good long while. It looked to be stirring up some kind of suicidal whirlpool.

#137606. A Bear to Be Thankful For: I Hunted a Record Black Bear on Thanksgiving Day

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3518 w)
