  • Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • Industry observers note that so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

Industry observers note that so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

Industry observers note that these nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

Sources indicate that ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

If the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

Industry observers note that issues with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “proposal falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

Sources indicate that what if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

If pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

In a recent development, the boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

Recent findings suggest that for maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

It has been revealed that an alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

Recent findings suggest that have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

Sources indicate that if it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

Sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

The biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

Many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

In a recent development, the most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

Industry observers note that the quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

It has been revealed that if those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

Once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

The lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

Now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

If the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

Industry observers note that if you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

Sources indicate that once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

Even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid big swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

According to recent reports, if a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

Besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

On coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

Industry observers note that let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

With both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done promptly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

Technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a massive, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

In a recent development, there are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

Lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is vital.

Industry observers note that lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

But, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the issue being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

If you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

Recent findings suggest that but what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

While you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a new stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

But what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

Recent findings suggest that I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is important. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

In a recent development, lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

If the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

If the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

Recent findings suggest that however, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

According to recent reports, speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

According to recent reports, I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

The climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

Recent findings suggest that see? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

Fractals in the Dirt

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, not long ago, I drove six hours with the Mancos Shale riding shotgun.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s how it goes across great swaths of Latest Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Wyoming, and Utah.
  • This story — and 42 issues of them — opens with a subscription.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, not long ago, I drove six hours with the Mancos Shale riding shotgun. That isn’t a buddy’s quirky nickname, as in: Yo, my man Mancos, my Shaley bro, hand me the Doritos and Sour Patch Kids, would ya please? It is in fact a geologic formation, a remarkably friable gray-blue-brown mudstone deposited in the Late Cretaceous, some ninety million years before present, when much of what we today call the American West was inundated by a vast inland sea. To an unsuspecting bystander, a turkey vulture or major-rig trucker, I must have seemed to be a lone soul on a desert road trip, only the radio’s pop divas, evangelical preachers, and static for company. Wrong. Mile after mile, the Mancos was at my side, catching the corner of my eye, whispering sweet nothings in my ear, keeping me intrigued and entertained.

Recent findings suggest that that’s how it goes across great swaths of Latest Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Wyoming, and Utah. The Mancos is here, there, everywhere—an.

#137593. The 7 Most Desperate Things I’ve Done in My Search for Ski Boots That Fit

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
📖 Baca

The 7 Most Desperate Things I’ve Done in My Search for Ski Boots That Fit

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • In a recent development, seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed.
  • Overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In a recent development, seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed. (Photo: Courtesy Abigail Barronian).

Overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage. It’s a funny account of what hard-to-fit feet can drive a person to do, and a reminder that the right bootfitter can change everything.

According to recent reports, in my quest for ski boots that fit, I’ve seen bootfitters in at least seven states and two countries. I’ve visited Evo and REI, small independent shops, local chains, and garages-turned-ski shops. I’ve consulted boot designers, brand reps, professional athletes, and gear reviewers; tried Intuitions, ZipFits, and custom footbeds. I’ve seen one orthopedic doctor, three acupuncturists, and two physical therapists. I’ve stayed up at night thinking about boots, and developed recurring stress dreams about them.

It has been revealed that last season, I was beginning to consider looping in a tarot reader or astrologer. Maybe I needed a psychotherapist, or a priest. Maybe I’d have to just quit skiing. And then, finally, I found my bootfitter. But not before resorting to some questionable behavior along the way. Here are seven desperate things I did in my search for a bootfitter who could solve my ski boot issues.

It has been revealed that every pair of ski boots I wore from ages two through 22 were hand-me-downs from my older brothers. Then I started working in the ski industry. While skiing around Massive Sky during a media event, a kind man working for Nordica looked at my feet with a frown.

“What are those?” he asked. I was sliding around in some decade-old size 26.5 monstrosities. He shook his head and invited me to swing by the Nordica headquarters in Upcoming Hampshire. There, he measured my feet and sent me off with a pair of 25.5 Nordica Promachines.

Everything changed. Suddenly I was in an aggressive stance, my shins met real resistance, my power transfer improved dramatically. I got a taste of what a good boot can do, shortly before developing a wicked case of tendonitis in my ankles and shins.

It has been revealed that after two seasons of excruciating, day-ending pain, I booked an appointment with an orthopedic foot and ankle specialist. I knew my boots were the culprit, and couldn’t be sure a doctor would understand the whole foot-encased-in-rigid-plastic thing. I lugged a giant bag with both my alpine and touring boots into the orthopedic practice and pulled them out for show-and-tell.

The physician kindly assured me he knew what ski boots were, and that I wasn’t dealing with any serious medical issues. I’d have to take my boots back where they belonged.

The owner of Santa Fe’s one dedicated ski shop sized me down yet again, into the stiffest 24.5 he had on hand—a 110 from Fischer. I felt like I was skiing in socks and a vise-grip at the same time, and I lost feeling in my feet on the first lap. Mercifully, he let me return them.

I’d hit the central problem: boots big enough to be comfortable gave me tendonitis, and boots small enough to prevent it gave me bunions and nerve pain. So I took my boots to Taos Bootdoctors, where a whole team of bootfitters worked patiently to expand the forefoot. I’d ski for a day or two and come back, over and over, looking for just a few more millimeters. I brought six-packs and did my best to be charming, and the lovely staff never made me feel less vital than the tourists dropping thousands of dollars on gear. Still, I couldn’t finish a day without pain.

I soldiered through the season, eyeing an upcoming hut trip with dread. I could manage shorter tours, but a week of daylong missions posed some real problems. Once we were in the mountains, I knew no amount of bunion donuts and anti-inflammatories would save me. I had to instate boots-off breaks in the middle of eight-hour ski days, carefully pulling my socked feet out of jail and propping them up on a backpack in the snow while my friends took an extra lap. Sweet, stupid relief.

Finally, I heard a rumor about a man in Seattle working out of his garage who was willing to do unorthodox things to ski boots. He had a history of custom-fitting plug boots for ski racers, which seemed like a good sign. While visiting family in Washington, I brought him both pairs of boots.

Industry observers note that he looked at my feet, listened patiently, and rattled off a comprehensive proposal that involved several devices I’d never seen before. Overnight, he molded both pairs into a completely new shape. I never had to touch either boot again, and proceeded with great pleasure to ski 12-hour days in the backcountry and endless resort laps with happy feet. I had found him—the bootfitter I was looking for. Then, he retired.

When my touring boots started to go, I bought a replacement pair and nobody could make them fit. The experience began to take on mythic proportions. I felt like the princess with a pea beneath her many mattresses, or an ugly stepsister trying to cram her foot into a crystal slipper: all discomfort and wrong fit.

Sources indicate that it seemed my trusty Tecnicas were the problem. I tried on every touring boot at ski shops in three states. I ordered over a dozen pairs online, obsessively double-checking return policies and momentarily racking up a very scary credit card bill. Eventually, I came crawling back to my old Tecnicas with no plan, two full seasons into the search.

Sources indicate that I hesitated to say yes to ski trips, afraid I’d have to sit out ski days because of pain or busted gear. Eventually, it happened: I took my tired old touring boots to Rogers Pass in B.C. and, on day three, broke the upper cuff clean off the bottom section of the boot. Thankfully we were just a few hundred yards from the truck. I spent the entire day sitting at the trailhead.

In the meantime, my alpine boots had begun to warp. I found a replacement pair and was back at square one: home in New Mexico, with two pairs of ski boots that didn’t fit, rapidly dwindling patience, and no bootfitter.

I considered that this might be the end of the road for me as a skier. Then, I learned that one of the best skiers I know had been contemplating quitting the sport because of foot pain. He’d even gone so far as to teach himself to snowboard. But then he found exactly what I’d been looking for: yet another fit-obsessed industry veteran working out of his garage.

Sources indicate that I visited another home workshop in western Washington and the bootfitter listened carefully as I explained the issue. Then, he overhauled both pairs of boots, tirelessly stretching the forefoots to give my feet room to breathe. They took on a completely fresh shape: generous and wide. I took both pairs out for a spin and sighed in relief.

There are a lot of great bootfitters out there. But for a freak like me, I’ve learned I need something of a mad scientist. If you’re plagued with bone spurs, high insteps, wide feet—there’s hope, I promise. With a little faith, a lot of persistence, and maybe something like divine intervention, I trust you’ll find the bootfitter you need. Let’s just hope they don’t retire.

#137592. Breaking: Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1545 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
  • In a recent development, now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.
  • Industry observers note that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

In a recent development, now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

Industry observers note that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”.

Actually, big is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a fresh best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

There’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

In a recent development, “I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a substantial challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

It has been revealed that finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

Recent findings suggest that she also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

It has been revealed that the setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

It has been revealed that “I just set it and left it,” she remarked. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

“I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she said. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty massive disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

In a recent development, her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

According to recent reports, “As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she said. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

She never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

“I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she noted. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

It has been revealed that working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

“I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she noted of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

It has been revealed that she also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling strategy: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

In a recent development, instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

“There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

As Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she said.

Beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

According to recent reports, and in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

“I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case said. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.

#137590. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (865 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm.
  • Industry observers note that this is a film review of sorts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

There is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

Industry observers note that this is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

In a recent development, but can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

It has been revealed that however, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a big-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

My reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

It has been revealed that I watched The Alpinist on the significant screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

It has been revealed that but anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

It has been revealed that from my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

Nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (752 w)

This Massive Swordfish Smashed the State Record, But It Was Disqualified Over a Technicality

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jake Kinzie had a crew of three buddies aboard his 28-foot boat while fishing off Ocean City, Maryland the morning of November 11.
  • Swordfish action has been good this year along the Atlantic Coast.
  • In 1,000 feet of water, they put out a swordfish squid bait on a 10/0 Mustad hook, taken deep with a strobe light attached to the leader to get the attention of a heavy fish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, capt. Jake Kinzie had a crew of three buddies aboard his 28-foot boat while fishing off Ocean City, Maryland the morning of November 11. The anglers ran 60 miles out to fish the deep “Poorman’s Canyon” for prized swordfish — and they would end up catching the largest sword in state history.

Swordfish action has been good this year along the Atlantic Coast. And the “Way Out” crew had caught a couple substantial swords earlier off Ocean City.

In 1,000 feet of water, they put out a swordfish squid bait on a 10/0 Mustad hook, taken deep with a strobe light attached to the leader to get the attention of a heavy fish.

Recent findings suggest that “Jake is an old friend I’ve known for over two decades,” Capt. Keith Jacobs tells Outdoor Life. “We were with our other buddies Joe Spayd and Blaine Beyer, and about 2:30 p.m. we hooked a deep, very large fish.”.

It has been revealed that spayd was on the rod, fighting the tough swordfish for about three hours. It never jumped, and the anglers never saw it until late in the fight.

Recent findings suggest that “We knew it was huge because it was so powerful,” says Jacobs, a professional boat captain and owner of “OC-anic,” a fishing gear and apparel organization. “But we figured it was only 300 pounds or so until we saw it near the boat as the sun was setting.”.

Jacobs noted it was all they could do to keep the swordfish from getting close to their boat and perhaps breaking the 80-pound test braided line on the Daiwa reel that Spayd used. He fought the fish from a gunnel rod holder on a swivel.

Sources indicate that “Jake had to spin the boat a lot to keep the line from rubbing against the boat hull,” Jacobs states. “Three hours into the fight we got the fish close to our boat, but it was still full of fight.”.

According to recent reports, while Spayd stayed on the rod battling the sword, Beyer hit the fish with a harpoon dart. The metal dart head, with a heavy line fitted to it, detached from the pole.

“Then I hit the fish in the head with a massive gaff – which wasn’t such a good idea,” says Jacobs. “It went crazy and ripped the gaff handle out of my hands and we lost it overboard.”.

Jacobs hit the fish with another gaff to help control and kill it.

Industry observers note that “We struggled to get a tail rope around the fish,” Jacobs says. “All that time lines were crossing, we’re wet, tired, the fish is thrashing beside the boat – and it’s getting dark in three-foot seas.”.

In a recent development, finally, the anglers secured the massive swordfish with a tail rope. After the fish died, they had to haul it into their 28-foot boat.

It has been revealed that “We didn’t have a block-and-tackle or come-along, so we had to grab it and haul it over the stern and around the boat’s two outboards,” Jacobs says. “We had to do it twice, because a fin got wedged in one of the outboards.

“We were exhausted when we finally got it in the boat. It took up about half of the deck space. That’s when we headed back in to Ocean City.”.

According to recent reports, the anglers arrived at Ocean City’s Snug Harbor waterfront neighborhood about 9 p.m. There the 12-foot long fish was hauled out of their boat with a crane and weighed on a digital scale at 558 pounds.

Industry observers note that it topped the largest swordfish caught by a sport angler by 165 pounds. That fish was boated in 2022 by angler Jeff Jacobs and weighed 393 pounds.

Read Next: Maine Tuna Fisherman Accidentally Catches Record-Setting Swordfish.

The anglers covered their 558-pound swordfish with fish bags and ice, and the next day contacted authorities to enter it as a state record catch.

Sources indicate that “But we learned that because we used an electric Daiwa reel it doesn’t qualify as a Maryland record,” Jacobs says. “Other states have record fish that are certified if electric reels are used by sporting tackle anglers.

“The tackle we used – even with electric reels – is far different than what commercial fishermen use.

“I wish Maryland had another records division that allows electric reels for heavyweight marine gamefish like swordfish, tuna, and giant marlin.”.

Tech Report: LaCrosse Alphaburly Aero 2000 Boot Review: The Warmest Boot LaCrosse Has Ever Made

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Recent findings suggest that insulated rubber boots are warm and waterproof.
  • In a recent development, last week I got the chance to field test LaCrosse’s new Alphaburly Aero 2000 insulated rubber boot on a whitetail hunt in Saskatchewan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that insulated rubber boots are warm and waterproof. But they’re also heavy, hard to walk in, and uncomfortable to wear for a long period of time — or at least they used to be.

In a recent development, last week I got the chance to field test LaCrosse’s new Alphaburly Aero 2000 insulated rubber boot on a whitetail hunt in Saskatchewan. The program for this kind of hunt is as follows: A cheery Canadian guide drops you off at a ground blind somewhere way back in the bush; you sit there overlooking a small shooting window from dark to dark; you never leave the blind because the biggest buck of your life could show up at any moment.

Temperatures on this hunt ranged from the mid 20s to low 40s, which is chilly but not as cold as we were hoping for (temps in the teens with a good foot of snow really get the bucks moving during daylight up there, or at least so I’ve heard).

Recent findings suggest that this was the perfect testing ground for a rubber boot that’s designed for cold-weather deer hunting, among other duties. Here’s how the newly introduced LaCrosse boots held up.

The heart of the Aero line is the ETPU midsole, which borrows its design from the high-performance running world. The midsole returns energy as your foot strikes the ground (or more simply put, the boots are springy). The effect is that the boots are incredibly comfortable to walk in. If you’ve ever walked, say a mile or so in heavy boots, you know that they can wear out your legs and feet quickly. But with the upcoming LaCrosse design, the weight of the boots is offset by the springiness of the midsole.

But your feet won’t stay comfortable long if they’re cold. It’s common for rubber boot wearers to get sweaty feet early in the day, and then freeze later on. To combat this, LaCrosse is using a completely fresh type of insulation called Solarcore. This is a kind of aerogel, which is woven into the interior of the boot. It’s promoted as a very light, very warm kind of insulation. In fact these boots are up to a pound lighter than other insulated rubber boots in their class. That lighter weight makes them easier to walk in as well. Importantly, Solarcore also repels water, unlike Thinsulate. So if your feet do get sweaty or wet inside the boot, that moisture doesn’t soak into the insulation.

There is a Pro version of the boot, which is all rubber, but I prefer the neoprene. I think it’s more comfortable on those long, all day sits.

Industry observers note that there’s also an 800g insulation version of the boot if you don’t anticipate hunting in very cold weather. If you’re going to mostly be hunting in the mid-20s and 30s, I’d say you’d be fine with the 800g boot. If you’re hunting in temps below that, or your feet get cold easily, go with the max insulation.

Industry observers note that during any long sit in the cold, your feet and hands are most likely to get cold first. But over the four days that I hunted, essentially sitting still for 10 hours at a time, my feet never got cold. I wore a light wool sock with a heavy wool sock over it. No foot warmers. No heater. I was impressed with how well the Solarcore insulation worked.

Industry observers note that after the Saskatchewan hunt I took the boots to my family deer camp in Wisconsin and did a morning of still hunting with them. As advertised, they were extremely comfortable to walk in. I stepped in a stream that was shin deep and stood in it for about 2 minutes (just as a test) and experienced no leaks.

It has been revealed that only time will tell how these boots will hold up over the long term. I think one benefit of the full rubber Pro version is durability. Any sort of neoprene can wear out with hard use. So if you’re planning on hiking in these boots in any sort of rugged terrain, you’d want to go with the Pro version.

Recent findings suggest that these are expensive boots, but they are jam packed with new technology. They are a true upgrade from basic insulated rubber boots that we’ve all worn in the past. If you hunt in cold weather, if you want to walk comfortably in rubber boots, or if your feet get cold easily, the Alphaburly Aero 2000 is a good option to consider.

According to recent reports, I’m a Midwesterner who likes winter and I think I could wear these boots in zero degree temps without fear of getting cold. If you really wanted a bulletproof setup, pair these boots with a pair of heated socks and never get cold feet again.

#137584. Tech Report: Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

📅 26 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2079 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adventure-journal ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

📅 26 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adventure-journal

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.
  • Sources indicate that flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own.
  • Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Sources indicate that flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”.

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Industry observers note that ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

It has been revealed that in the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Recent findings suggest that our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

In a recent development, because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

Industry observers note that A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Industry observers note that among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”.

According to recent reports, whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of upcoming roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

Sources indicate that with the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and highlighted me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

According to recent reports, “They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”.

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

It has been revealed that on his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a upcoming rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

Industry observers note that ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

Sources indicate that I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the latest nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

Latest Update: Mountain Lion Is the Ultimate Underrated Game Meat. Here’s How to Prepare It
