A Thanksgiving Blizzard Pushed Massive Mule Deer Off the Mountain — and Down to Us

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The Buck and The Great Gray Owl,” appeared in the November 1972 matter of Outdoor Life.
  • For at least a mile, I had trudged along a U.S.
  • In a recent development, but following the trail wasn’t always easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The Buck and The Great Gray Owl,” appeared in the November 1972 matter of Outdoor Life.

For at least a mile, I had trudged along a U.S. Forest Service trail to avoid hunting through the dense evergreen woods on both sides. There the trees sagged under heavy burdens of snow, and to brush against just one branch was to release a load of it down the back of my neck.

In a recent development, but following the trail wasn’t always easy. In places the blaze marks were obliterated by snow that a high wind had plastered against the tree trunks, and here and there drifts were piled waist-high. Slogging through such deep wet snow can take the joy out of deer hunting, so I decided to head back for the warmth and comfort of the ranch. I elected to take a shortcut rather than to retrace my steps, and that decision proved to be a mistake.

My shortcut led down and around a slope, then crossed an old burned area, now grown up in a thicket, where the new snow covered a nightmare of crisscrossed deadfalls. Before I reached the far side of the burn, I tripped many times and was wet from chest to toes. I swore out loud the last time I fell, and in that instant three does suddenly sprung from their beds in the snow and fled downhill.

The does did not bounce away in the characteristic stiff-legged manner of mule deer. Instead they hesitated and floundered, now and then up to their bellies in the snow. I threw the rifle to my shoulder and could easily have shot all three, so slow was their progress. But the purpose of my trip was to bag one good buck, and I had a few more days to hunt.

Back in camp, I found George Smith and John Moxley propping wet boots close to a cast-iron stove to dry while a pot of coffee brewed on top.

“Did you see any game?” I asked.

“Not even a newly introduced track,” George answered.

“We may have started this hunt too late,” John added.

I almost had to agree with John — the three does were the only deer I had seen since arriving at George Smith’s Canyon Creek Ranch. For years George has been guiding hunters from this ranch, located in the Pioneer Mountains of the Beaverhead National Forest, about 17 miles of steep winding road from Melrose, Montana. When John and I couldn’t make our annual Western hunt in time for the October opening of the major-game season, George suggested that we hold off until the season’s last week, which would be the last week in November.

It has been revealed that “By that time,” he had written, “the substantial bucks should be down low and we can have a real trophy hunt. Besides, all my guests will have gone home for Thanksgiving, so Bob and I can join you.”.

Bob is my youngest son, and he was working for the Smith family during the season as a guide and wrangler.

The proposal sounded perfect to John and me. John is from Ohio, and I had recently moved from Ohio to Wyoming.

On a crisp bright day in November — perfect weather for big-game hunting — I met John at the airport in Butte, Montana. We picked up some supplies and then drove the 60 miles to Canyon Creek Ranch. We arrived well after dusk under a still-clear sky.

In a recent development, I’d never felt more optimistic about starting a hunt. But two things did bother me. First, we did not see any deer in the headlights of our vehicle on the drive to the ranch. Second, after our arrival George mentioned seeing a great gray owl around the ranch buildings. In that region the great gray is a rare visitor, and according to George it arrives only ahead of a storm.

“The last gray owl I saw,” George recalled, “came just before the worst winter storm in my memory hit this place.”.

Late that night, snow began to fall and a violent wind came up. The snow didn’t stop until more than a foot of white covered the high country — about 7,000 feet at the Canyon Creek Ranch — and the temperature plunged to zero. We did very little hunting, and it was unsuccessful.

According to recent reports, “The deer have either bedded down until the blast passes,” George explained, “or moved down to where the snow isn’t so deep. We’ll have to wait and see.”.

According to recent reports, at first the waiting wasn’t too bad. I hadn’t seen Bob or George for a year, and we had plenty of stories to swap in the snug ranch atmosphere. Besides, there was a Thanksgiving banquet to cook and eat. But eventually I got restless and wanted to start hunting in spite of the conditions. The result was that we left a good many bootprints in the deep snow without covering much distance or seeing any deer or even any game sign.

In a recent development, the morning after I saw the does, I started out early. The wind had stopped blowing, but visibility was still poor. Gray clouds hung in the canyons and close to the wooded slopes so that long-range scanning with binoculars was seldom possible. One very effective tactic for hunting in good snow cover in mountainous country is to carefully glass all slopes, particularly south slopes, for game that stands out sharply against the white. The clouds ruled out that tactic.

But the day didn’t pass without excitement. I had crossed a steep draw and, on reaching level ground on the far side, had paused to catch my breath. A moment later I heard animals crashing toward me through an evergreen thicket up ahead. My heart began to pound. I flipped off the safety on my Model 700 Remington 7 mm. Magnum and held the rifle ready. A cow moose followed by a calf stomped into the open and crossed my path without even a sidelong glance in my direction. It was quite a surprise to see them so far from more-typical moose habitat.

Industry observers note that bob had good news back at the ranch that night. He had scouted in another direction and found many tracks.

Recent findings suggest that “They seem to be paralleling Canyon Creek, heading down toward the old ghost camp,” Bob remarked. “If the snow’s thinner, we might find them there tomorrow.”.

The next morning was bitterly cold. We gathered in the ranch kitchen and huddled around the cook stove while George carved thick strips of bacon from a slab and mixed up a large bowl of sourdough pancake batter. It is a standard practical joke around Canyon Creek to conceal a round sheet of cardboard inside some unsuspecting diner’s pancake and then watch him try to cut it with a fork. George pulled the trick on John, and we had a good laugh before beginning a cold day.

Industry observers note that it was possible to drive our four-wheel-drive rig partway to where Bob had found sign the day before. We parked our vehicle beside a small tributary of Canyon Creek, now almost completely frozen, and followed it on foot to an open meadow bordered by a wooded slope. There we found Bob’s tracks as well as deer tracks that had been made since his reconnaissance. It was soon evident that a herd of deer had fed along the meadow’s edges; in windswept places they had pawed circular areas free of snow to get at the vegetation underneath. But apparently the deer hadn’t lingered long, and their tracks disappeared in many different directions.

“Our best bet,” George said, “is to go separate ways and see what we find.”.

Because George knew the country best, he took a more complicated route, which led through heavy cover, wound around a mountainside, and nearly dead-ended at a steep rocky cliff. He figured that game might be bedded on top or near the face of the cliff.

Industry observers note that john and I proceeded together until the meandering tracks appeared to divide into two small herds. Then we separated, planning to meet late in the day on an unimproved road far below.

Sources indicate that one set of the tracks I followed was very large, and I concentrated on it. I walked parallel to the buck’s path on the downwind side while watching far ahead for a glimpse of the animal. That technique had worked well for me on other hunts, and it might work again.

It has been revealed that I was so intent on following the buck that I almost stumbled over a bedded doe. She went flying in a cloud of snow down the slope. Then, before my hands were steady again, a shot cracked in the distance. The shot spooked a second deer about 150 yards to my right. I saw the animal for only an instant and couldn’t tell whether it was my buck. But when I hurried back to the buck’s trail, I found the spot where he had suddenly shifted into high gear.

For the rest of the day I stillhunted slowly but got no action. I was optimistic, however, for at last we were in deer country.

Sources indicate that the shot I’d heard was George’s. He had broken the ice. About a mile from where he’d left John and me, he’d noticed that the tracks of the largest deer became more meandering — often an indication that a deer is seeking a good place to bed. George slowed his own pace accordingly, stopping often to scan thoroughly every bit of mountain terrain in front of him. This is the simplest and oldest of all mule-deer-hunting strategies, and once again it paid off.

Just before George reached a small draw, he stopped. Soon he saw a shape that put him on alert. On the slope slightly above him was the outline of a buck’s rack, somewhat obscured by a screen of brush. In the next moment the deer was on its feet and running. But it was slowed by snow, and it hadn’t gone more than 20 feet when George drilled a shot through the lungs. He found the animal dead 50 yards from where it had been hit.

Industry observers note that the buck was an old, heavy five-pointer (Western count) with unusually heavy beams. It was a trophy that even an old-timer in the Montana Rockies could brag about. The buck, even when field-dressed, was a terrible weight to drag to the nearest pickup point. Without the slippery snow and all-downhill going, we would have needed a packhorse or two for the job.

Sources indicate that but the day produced more than a trophy mule deer for George. It also revealed that deer were moving from the high country into lower ranges where food was more available. The farther we had hunted that day, the more fresh tracks we had encountered. John reported jumping 12 deer from a sheltered meadow that, from the amount of tracks and digging in the snow, resembled a livestock pasture. None of the deer had the kind of rack that John was looking for, but his gloom early in the trip had been replaced by enthusiasm.

“Tomorrow,” he predicted to me, “both of us will score.”.

It has been revealed that the next morning was overcast, and flurries of snow drifted to the ground as we huddled again around the kitchen stove. After breakfast George drove us to a spot close to where John had seen deer the day before. We had driven along that same trail several times before. Only two days before, John noted, the only track on the upcoming snow had been made by a wandering coyote. Now deer tracks were everywhere.

George left John and me where the road forked. He would pick us up late in the afternoon at a point about two miles farther on.

In a recent development, few thrills can match walking through woodlands that you know contain game. You are tense and excited, and it’s difficult to slow down and hunt carefully enough.

According to recent reports, john and I had scarcely separated when I saw deer running over an open ridge ahead and above me. I didn’t spot any antlers, but no matter. All the animals were out of range and gone before I would have had a shot.

“Slow down,” I remarked to myself half-aloud. But my pulse was racing.

It has been revealed that that day I saw as many muleys as I’ve ever seen on a day’s hunt afoot. We had found a winter deer yard, and collecting venison would have been incredibly easy. But I kept hoping for the significant buck. Actually I did see two together, but they were traveling and already 400 to 500 yards away.

Industry observers note that at dusk when I came out again on the road, weary to the bone, I still hadn’t fired a shot. The headlights of George’s vehicle were a welcome sight in the gloom. Even better was the significant buck lashed on top. John had scored, and back at the ranch he told about it.

According to recent reports, early in the morning, after his eagerness had spooked a very good buck, John decided to hunt more from the seat of his pants and less by hiking all over the landscape. When he found a good sheltered place, he sat down on a deadfall. Though the mountain slope opposite him seemed empty of game, he studied it through his glasses. Soon he focused on a spike buck, bedded and almost hidden behind a juniper bush. John shifted his gaze slightly upward, and there he saw the kind of buck he wanted.

The four-pointer was bedded in a cluster of trees and was in deep shadow. But his antlers, outlined against the snow, gave him away. John figured that the range was more than 500 yards — much too far to risk a shot — but that by making good use of the cover on his side of the mountain he could cut the distance in half. He made the stalk successfully, and one shot from his Model 700 Remington .30/06 anchored the buck.

That left one day — the last day of the open season — for me to score.

Perhaps because of the intense cold in the bunkhouse the next morning, the alarm clock didn’t work and George had to awaken me.

“Look out the window,” he called, “and over toward Canyon Creek.”.

There, in the crown of a dead spruce splintered long ago by lightning, sat the great gray owl. Probably another storm was on its way. As a result I wolfed my breakfast and, though I should have known better, got hooked on one of George’s cardboard pancakes.

Recent findings suggest that george drove me close to the deer yard we had found, and from there I started out on foot. It was not a pleasant morning to be afield. Scattered snow flurries were being driven by a wild bitter wind, which was promptly obliterating deer tracks and which made cautious hunting — stopping often to scan the slopes — very difficult. I had to keep moving to keep warm. By mid-morning I had found very few fresh tracks and had seen no deer. I figured that all or at least most of the deer had already moved to even lower elevations ahead of the new storm. My chances looked very poor.

Sources indicate that at noon I found some deadfalls on the edge of a dense spruce thicket that furnished a fairly good windbreak, and I sat down to munch a sandwich and a candy bar. The place also gave me a good view, between snow squalls, of distant, partly timbered mountainsides. Through binoculars I examined the wooded slopes, concentrating on those farthest away. As I glassed, I caught a slight movement much closer. Refocusing the glasses, I saw a forkhorn traveling slowly down the hill below me. He was less than 200 yards away, and though the crosswind wasn’t the best for shooting, it would not give me away.

In a recent development, I decided I would have to take the forkhorn or get nothing at all. Slowly I raised my rifle and found a rest for it on the deadfall. The shot would have been easy, but as I was about to squeeze off, a second forkhorn strolled out into the open. Then, right behind him, came a third buck.

At first I could see only the body of the third buck in my scope. But that was enough to tell me he was big. As I watched, the buck changed direction and was hidden from view again. Should I take a chance and play the waiting game, or shoot one of the forkhorns, still in sight?

Industry observers note that the massive buck resolved my indecision when he appeared again. This time I could see his splendid rack. My 7 mm. was sighted-in for 200 yards, so I held the crosshairs on the point of the shoulder, adjusted for windage, and squeezed. The deer lurched forward, out of view; I didn’t know whether I’d connected.

I hurried down the steep slope and waded through a deep drift in a gully. I found the buck lying dead against a tree trunk. He was a fine four-pointer and as heavy a mule deer as I’ve ever bagged.

Recent findings suggest that that evening the great gray owl proved to be an accurate prophet. Another storm pounded the Rockies and plastered the high country with another layer of snow. But back at the ranch, I barely noticed it.

“The idea of the late hunt,” John noted, “was sure a great one.”.

A Montana nonresident big-game license costs $151. A deer-only license, which entitles the holder to one deer in a specified district, is $35, plus $1 for a conservation license. This year the general season on deer in Montana runs from October 22 to November 26. But prospective hunters should write the Montana Fish and Game Department, Helena, Montana 59601, for a copy of the detailed hunting regulations.

Read Next: I Promised to Take My Boys Rabbit Hunting Every Day of Christmas Break.

Sources indicate that the tag end of the season can be a good time for any big-game hunt. Almost everywhere in the West, the odds for connecting with a trophy head may be improved then, simply because the animals are not so high and are easier to find. Of course, there are unseasonably warm years when animals are not driven downward by deep snow until after the season ends. Remember too that late-season hunting can be very rugged — and occasionally impossible. It’s wise to know bad-weather and snow-survival techniques. But these are the chances a sportsman must take. And for my money, the rewards are worth the gamble.

Latest Update: Hunting Unpressured Bucks on One of the Best Properties in the Country

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we are well into deer season now, and bucks are definitely feeling the pressure. If you’re like the rest of us, you’re probably seeing daylight movement start to decrease on your trail cameras, or maybe it’s already dropped off. I’m right there with you. The places that I hunt see plenty of pressure, even though they’re on private ground. This week on the podcast, I’m talking to our gear editor, Scott Einsmann, who just came back from an incredibly unique experience: He was hunting almost completely unpressured mature bucks in the Midwest. Scott shares what that experience was like, what he learned from it, and how it can help him — and you — back in the real world of deer hunting. —Alex Robinson, editor-in-chief.

Listen to this episode on Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Recent findings suggest that alex Robinson: Hey, Scott, thanks for joining the Outdoor Life Podcast. I want to talk to you about your favorite thing in the world, which is bowhunting for whitetail deer.

Industry observers note that scott Einsmann: Awesome. Let’s do it. I just came off the most amazing week of bowhunting for whitetails.

According to recent reports, alex: Yeah. We’re coming up on the holiday season, and you have a good redemption story, and everybody loves a good redemption story around the holidays. So to start this off, explain the property that you’re able to hunt in Illinois. What’s it like, and how did you weasel your way into getting bowhunting access to this place?

Scott: It’s 800 acres in southern Illinois, and what makes it a really good 800 acres is, one, it has topography, and it also has large wood blocks in it, and it’s surrounded by massive ag fields. So once all the crops are cut, all the deer get sucked right into this property. For that reason, it’s just insane hunting. There are really good deer. There’s not a 200-incher on it, but there are a ton of 130- to 150-inch deer, and a ton of really good 8-points — some really cool deer. Last year, some big 6-points were killed, which is always fun. And maybe 300 does just running around this place. I mean, it’s crazy.

Alex: So talk about whose property it is and how you’re able to get on it, because you’re not a multimillionaire property owner.

Alex: A lot of these properties are either owned or leased by — you know, it’s the stuff that everybody dreams about hunting, but not everybody really gets access to.

Scott: Yes. And I did inquire with the farm manager there: How does someone get a lease in this area? You really just have to know the local farmers, because a lot of them have been burned by people leasing their property and not treating it right. So you really have to have someone to vouch for you and then be part of the community.

It has been revealed that luckily, I know someone. Levi Morgan and Andy Morgan have the lease for this property, and they have several leases in the area now, and they’re all pretty incredible. But this one they’ve had the longest — about three years now — and they’re really starting to dial it in and understand how the deer use it. They’re connected with our friends at Tactacam Reveal, and part of being an outdoor writer is you get to go on press trips.

Industry observers note that press trips vary in quality and fun. But this one is by far the best I’ve ever been on, because it’s not a guided hunt. You’re not just being driven around by an outfitter and sitting over a corn pile somewhere. We go out there in the summer, we hang stands, we hang cameras, get to learn the property a little bit, and then we have access to those cameras all season long — which for me is great, because my home lease is not that exciting by comparison.

Scott: So just being able to scroll and see cool deer after cool deer — and they have a ton of turkeys as well, and I have some good news there. So we have access to all that, and then we come back in November and hunt the place during the peak of the rut.

Now deer hunters everywhere use these tried-and-true tactics. We take a look back to when these trusty standbys were still considered downright bizarre.

It has been revealed that the brush-country hunters of Texas and Latest Mexico were crashing antlers together for decades before the trend caught fire in the rest of whitetail country. Although Native hunters almost certainly developed the technique, legend has it that an old market hunter accidentally discovered the phenomenon.

Sources indicate that “He was coming to town one day, his wagon loaded with deer carcasses, when a buck came barging out of the mesquite,” reads one May 1951 story from OL. “The hunter, so the story goes, added him to the load. A short time later, another buck pranced up — and was soon in the wagon. The puzzled hunter stopped to figure things out and discovered that two carcasses were lying so their antlers clashed as the wagon jounced along the rough country road.”.

Related: How to Rattle in a Buck, Based on Whitetail Deer Research.

It has been revealed that our first story devoted to rattling appeared in October 1937. A Texas game warden, drawing on 30 years of experience with the tactic, taught author Fredric P. Schwab exactly how to sound like “two bucks in a life-and-death struggle.”.

By the 1950s, most hunters in the rest of the country had heard of rattling, but few had tried it. Almost everyone who had tried tickling tines reported the method didn’t work on hill-country deer, although a rare hunter outside the Lone-Star State would claim success. Here’s what modern research says about the efficacy of rattling in deer.

The concept of calling for deer was less established even than rattling in the middle of the 20th century. In August 1949, an experienced deer hunter traveled to Alaska for a Sitka blacktail hunt. “He was sure it was just a gag,” reads the story. “Who ever head of calling a buck?”.

“Now I’ve used crow calls, duck calls, and turkey calls, and I’d read that down in Texas they lure bucks by rattling a couple of antlers together. But a real deer call I’d never heard of. Probably my voice expressed my skepticism. ‘O.K. I’ll bite. What’s a deer call?’”.

Read Now: When and How to Use a Grunt Tube to Call in Deer.

The Alaskan hunters employed the call often — which looks a bit like a harmonica and sounds like “a lost lamb bleating for its mother,” — but they admit they don’t know what sound it was supposed to replicate. “I’ve attracted does as well as bucks, so I don’t think it’s a mating call,” noted one local. “An old Indian told me it’s the cry of a fawn in mortal terror,” said another.

In the end, the author and a fellow hunter call in two bucks and drop both of them. This story, “A Deer Call Brings ‘Em In!” garnered so much reader mail that an advice column on using commercial calls appeared in the August 1949 issue. The expert claimed to have used his call with excellent results on 100 wild deer, and that his call was a modern counterpart of those made by Native Americans in Alaska. So while calls were being produced commercially by the late 40s, they remained news to most hunters.

Although a variety of products designed to lure bucks and cover up human odor had been marketed for years, it appears most hunters initially considered the scents for sale at the local sporting goods shop akin to something hawked by a snake oil salesman.

Read Next: 15 Scent Control Strategies That Actually Work for Deer Hunting.

“It was probably because I was growing desperate that I decided to buy the deer scent,” writes John Weiss, author of the November 1978 feature “Scents and Nonscents.” “I figured there was nothing to lose.”.

Industry observers note that weiss reported that more than 50 companies made scents at the time, and were raking in an estimated $37 million a year. That included everything from hunter’s soaps and food attractants to tarsal scents and urine.

Sources indicate that he then delved into the types of scents and their effectiveness, and dug into the “scientific” realm of deer hunting. Interestingly, most biologists interviewed for the story disregarded “a deer’s scenting ability as not all that important.” One researcher noted that a deer’s “visual capabilities are far more refined than hearing or smelling abilities.”.

It has been revealed that yet most wildlife biologists today agree that a deer’s nose is it’s most formidable asset. Nonscents, indeed. It makes you wonder: If these are the facts we believed back then, just think about what we’ve got wrong now. And, even more fun to imagine, is what idiotic tactic might be all the rage in another couple decades.

Turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie, and football. In America, that’s usually what’s on the menu on the fourth Thursday in November. But in the fall of 1621, the original Thanksgiving meal didn’t resemble this in the slightest. The Pilgrims at Plymouth Plantation had a lot to be thankful for. The Wampanoag helped them survive the previous winter and harvest plenty of food over the summer. The two groups decided to come together and celebrate this for a few days with a feast, during which they ate a mix of wild fish and game. Here is an excerpt from one of two firsthand accounts from a man named Edward Winslow:.

Recent findings suggest that “Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors. They four in one day killed as much fowl as, with a little help beside, served the firm almost a week. At which time, amongst other recreations, we exercised our arms, many of the Indians coming amongst us, and among the rest their greatest king Massasoit, with some ninety men, whom for three days we entertained and feasted, and they went out and killed five deer, which they brought to the plantation and bestowed on our governor, and upon the captain and others.”.

According to recent reports, that sounds a little more like deer camp than grandma’s house. Along with a pile of venison and week’s supply of fowl, it’s not out of the question to assume there were also dried fruits, berries, nuts, fish, and shellfish at the feast. Instead, things like berries and other fruit had to be eaten fresh or preserved. The most likely way they would have done this is by drying, but there’s another way to preserve fruit without refrigeration. Canning has been done for generations, and it’s still a perfect way to preserve wild berries for months. The pilgrims wouldn’t have had the sugar for this wild black raspberry jam recipe, but it still goes good with butter and toast, on a leftover turkey sandwich, or even some acorn-flour pancakes.

According to recent reports, today lobsters and other shellfish are considered delicacies, but 400 years ago, they were a staple. The Atlantic coastline provided Wampanoag and the colonists with clams, mussels, and lobster. But there’s also another crustacean, readily available in freshwater, that’s just as worthy of dipping in clarified butter: the crayfish. Here’s a classic crayfish etouffee to serve alongside the main course.

In the first sentence of the Winslow account, there’s a mention of fowl:.

“Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors.”.

Sources indicate that turkey is considered fowl, but the first thanksgiving probably included waterfowl instead. Ducks and geese would have been easier for the settlers and the Wampanoag to catch and cook. They are also more plentiful in the wild. The birds were most likely roasted over a fire. Spit roasting a whole bird is an involved process, and most will opt for an oven instead, given a chance. Sources indicate that another bird readily available in the 17th century was the passenger pigeon. When populations were at their peak, it is stated that flocks were so thick they would black out the sky. Unfortunately, this didn’t last. Due to heavy market hunting and habitat loss, the passenger pigeon is now extinct. A similar bird (though not closely related) is the mourning dove. In fact, one of the last living wild passenger pigeons was found roosting with mourning doves.

Fish played a massive part in the colonist’s lives. They were loaned money to start the colony, and they planned to pay some of their debts back by fishing. Atlantic white cod would have been the fish of choice, though they would have also had access to other fish like runs Atlantic salmon. In a large pan, melt the butter over medium heat, add the shallots and garlic, and cook until soft (about 2 minutes). Season with a pinch of salt, and black pepper to taste. Add the wine and cook until almost all the wine is evaporated. Add the heavy cream and the parmesan and stir together, cooking until the cream thickens up a bit (1-2 minutes). Add the pasta and toss with the cream sauce. If the sauce is too thick, add some of the pasta water until you get a creamy sauce. Toss in the parsley, and serve topped with grated parmesan. This will make six healthy servings.

Deer meat was likely the centerpiece of the first thanksgiving. After all, the Wampanoag brought five deer with them to the feast. So where did this turkey thing come from anyway? The one other written account from the autumn of 1621 does mention that the pilgrims had turkey, although nobody is certain that it was eaten at the feast. The second account from William Bradford states:.

“And besides waterfowl there was great store of wild turkeys, of which they took many, besides venison, etc.”.

Long after Bradford’s death, his journal was found and reprinted in the 1850s, and for some reason, people really liked the part about turkey. During that time, Sarah Josepha Hale, the editor of a magazine called Godey’s Lady’s Book, promoted the turkey as a centerpiece of the table. Hale was also a strong voice behind Thanksgiving Day becoming a national holiday. She wrote letters and even petitioned a few presidents.

Finally, in 1863, Abraham Lincoln declared the day a national holiday, and turkey has been the star of the show ever since. Whether wild turkey was eaten during the first Thanksgiving or not, it’s still delicious. If you have a left-over gobbler from the spring, or one you’ve shot this fall, this wild take on a classic Thanksgiving turkey recipe is sure to get some attention at your table.

Industry observers note that gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Recent findings suggest that throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a fresh route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

Sources indicate that to Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions said. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

Colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management plan for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

According to recent reports, “There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher stated. Although that initial blueprint was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

As a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular major wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that sunday’s giant slalom will be a particularly tough test, with Brazil’s Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, the reigning Olympic GS champion and Crystal Globe winner, leading the field. Odermatt and Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard are also contenders to watch.

In a recent development, with the American men looking to build depth behind established veterans like Cochran-Siegle, Negomir is one to watch as the season progresses. A strong showing on home snow would be a substantial step forward.

Both men’s races stream live on Peacock and NBCSN. Saturday’s super-G coverage begins at 1:45 p.m. ET, and Sunday’s giant slalom starts at noon ET, with the second run at 3 p.m. ET. Spectators can watch in person; general admission is free.

One of the greatest ordeals of my life began on a bleak, heavily overcast day, with a strong north wind and temperatures never rising above 22°. Dr. George Dahnke and I, both of Memphis, had decided to hunt ducks in the Floodway over in Arkansas. We’d heard reports that mallards were swarming on Section 16 of the Floodway, and the ducks were there, as we were to learn the hard way.

The Floodway was still timberland. About 100,000 acres of it had been dammed and canalized to prevent the St. Francis River from flooding the towns of Marked Tree and Parkin. The forest floor was flooded all year, hence, the lure for ducks.

Industry observers note that george was an able physician and loyal friend, but he could never become a hunter. Though he was an enthusiast who tried hard, he began hunting too late in life and was too dedicated to the practice of medicine to give much thought to hunting. Further, he was not physically fit, being too soft through lack of exercise.

It has been revealed that we drove to the Floodway with my father-in-law, Mr. Ambrose, who was past 70 years of age. He realized that he was not up to the effort involved in as much boating as George and I planned to do, so he arranged for a local guide to paddle his boat and keep him close to the clubhouse.

This story, “I’ll Never Hunt Ducks Again,” appeared in the March 1982 glitch of Outdoor Life.

Industry observers note that george and I pushed off before daylight and began motoring with the current down the main ditch, No. 62, which flowed south. By dawn we’d gone about half the eight miles we intended to go. Long before we reached our goal we had seen enough flushing mallards to be reasonably sure of plenty of action. Finally we left the main ditch, No. 62, shut down the little outboard engine, and prepared to paddle west through the woods. The ducks continued to work overhead, seemingly intent on reaching the area we had chosen.

We found an ideal situation, where thick bunch brush, covered by a dense network of vines, overlooked half an acre of open water. We pushed the boat under that natural blind and broke out ports in the tangle so that we could fire from the boat. I threw six decoys into the shallow water, and the setup appeared to be ideal. The only problem was my apprehension that our limits would come too easily and promptly for the keenest sport.

The ducks flew high overhead in a constant stream but paid no attention to the invitations sounded on my Turpin call. I did my utmost to make every quack, chatter or chuckle perfect, but all the birds were homing in on one small area. Obviously, some other hunters had a better setup than we did.

It has been revealed that “George, those fellows are the lousiest callers I’ve ever heard,” I noted. “But they’re getting the ducks. Those fellows doing that tooting are champs for luck!”.

Related: Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure.

George blinked, then mentioned, “J.D., I hadn’t thought about it, but we can hear those jokers calling, and they’re no good.”.

“Yeah! And getting all the ducks!” I remarked, thoroughly disgusted. “Watch that bunch. They set their wings and are gliding straight in without circling.”.

I was envious, as well as curious. In all my years of duck hunting I had never encountered a similar situation.

According to recent reports, “Those guys sound like hogs feeding and hounds running,” George noted. “And geese honking, and cows lowing!” I added.

According to recent reports, suddenly I realized why the masses of ducks were heedless. “George,” I noted. “Those are ducks doing the calling! We have been sitting here like fools, criticizing the techniques of real ducks! What a dummy I am!”.

“How do you know they’re real ducks?” George asked.

“How many shots have you heard?” I stated. “If there were hunters over there, we would have heard them shooting.”.

Say, you’re right!” George said.

It has been revealed that “You stay here.” I suggested. “I’ll wade over and put that raft of ducks up. We can’t do any good as long as we have to compete with real ducks on the water.”.

Industry observers note that “Wait a minute, J.D.,” George mentioned. “Mind if I go with you? I never saw a big bunch of ducks on the water.”.

Industry observers note that before George was out of sight, the ducks came back in throngs. At first I merely gave the short call and the feed call, and the birds fell through the trees and onto the water in dozens, then in hundreds.

Industry observers note that three hundred yards of wading brought us to the mallard equivalent of the famous Antoine’s restaurant in New Orleans. Under the clear three to six-inch-deep water was a golden bed of acorns. There was scant time to absorb the charm of the place because about five acres of the area before us erupted into flight. The roar of at least 20,000 beating wings is best described by George’s reaction. Plucking at my sleeve he shouted, “Let’s get out of here. That’s a tornado!”.

“You can’t fool me,” he insisted. “I’m from Texas, remember? I know what tornados sound like!”.

“That’s the roar of duck wings you hear!” I said. “Ducks are making THAT much of a roar?” he shouted. We were forced to yell in order to be heard over the noise of the wings.

According to recent reports, as the ducks lifted out, the volume of sound diminished. “Where is your tornado now?” I asked.

Industry observers note that “That was unbelievable!” he said. “Simply incredible! Nobody could have made me understand that ducks could make that much noise, even if millions got up!”.

In a recent development, “George, this is the spot for our setup,” I noted. “If we had the boat and decoys here we could have a blue-ribbon shoot.”.

“Show me the direction of the boat and I’II go get it,” George mentioned.

Sources indicate that “OK,” I said, pointing his course. “Just keep that straight line and you can’t miss it.” He hitched his boots up in an instinctive gesture and ambled away. That decision to let George go after the boat was one of the most stupid of my mistakes. And it came nearest to being fatal.

Before George was out of sight, the ducks came back in throngs. At first I merely gave the short call and the feed call, and the birds fell through the trees and onto the water in dozens, then in hundreds. The ancient snag I leaned against provided ample cover because I remained motionless.

Recent findings suggest that soon the greedy mallards were feeding as though they could not gobble the acorns promptly enough. When my foot became cramped, I shifted slowly and slightly but the wary mallards were up and away.

It has been revealed that when some birds came back over and started circling I called them in and killed a pair. My motives were to give George a bearing. He had been away far longer than necessary and I began to be concerned.

The ducks were eager to get down to the feed, so killing the limit was absurdly easy. I decided that to work the crow call would give George my location. I blew the Turpin crow call as loudly as one has ever been sounded, confident that George would hear it and know who was calling. George was not a crow shooter, but he knew, or I thought he knew, there were none in the Floodway at that time of year.

Soon I became concerned about George, blaming myself for letting him fetch the boat. He was certainly no woodsman and even less a swamp rat. Just as I was trying to decide on a course of action, I heard the slosh, slosh of his deliberate wading. That was fine, except that he was approaching from the opposite direction than I had expected. I could see him quite plainly, in my imagination, as he splashed along towing the boat. When he actually appeared without the boat, I could hardly credit my senses.

“Where did you leave the boat?” I asked.

“I never did find it,” he noted.

Sources indicate that I felt as though I had been dealt a heavy blow between the eyes. I was dazed and disoriented. I was so thoroughly confused that I had to wade around three tall snags to find the 15 slain mallards I had tossed at the base of the substantial stump where I was standing. I had no idea where the boat was. The sky looked like the underside of a dark gray tent, precluding any possibility of gaining the least help from the sun. There were no traffic noises. No sound of whistles, bells or machinery was nearer than eight miles from us.

In a recent development, we found thousands upon thousands of wild mallards, but no trace of our six wooden decoys or any other clue to our boat’s location. As far as we were concerned, the boat had disappeared forever.

We were as hopelessly lost as though stranded in the Sahara or in forests of the Belgian Congo.

According to recent reports, I had my compass, but it was next to useless because no matter which direction we chose to follow, we could go only a short distance before we reached a deep ditch, canal or sink. All were filled with water, and we could swim across none. The only value of knowing the precise direction was to help us follow the only pathway that might wind around to provide the one route to the confluence of Ditch No. 62 and a string of borrow pits. It was there thal we just might luck onto someone in a boat, although the chance of any duck hunter being there so late in such weather was virtually nonexistent. I was scared — badly scared.

According to recent reports, without a boat we were doomed to remain in the flooded timber and die. We would become to weak to sit on a fallen tree trunk or to stand in the water, trying to balance ourselves on the muddy, uneven ground under the muddy, frigid water. Then we would freeze or drown.

In a recent development, our only hope was to find our boat. We found thousands upon thousands of wild mallards, but no trace of our six wooden decoys or any other clue to our boat’s location. As far as we were concerned, the boat had disappeared forever.

Recent findings suggest that this will give an indication of the futility of our search: After the ordeal I offered a trapper $10 to find the hidden boat. I explained as nearly as possible where the boat was, and he accepted the challenge. It was only after three days of careful, expert searching that he found it. He told us he’d passed within 10 yards of the craft three times — carefully following my directions — before he finally pushed the brush blind aside and found the boat.

“I never would have believed anybody could hide something as big as a boat, especially with wooden decoys floating on the water close to it, then tell me exactly where it was and I would have to look for it three days to find it,” he said.

Industry observers note that after abandoning our search for the boat, and our last hope of escaping from the flooded woods, I told George we would have to wade to where No. 62 ditch flowed past the borrow pits.

Should we by chance reach that point, we had a very slight chance to get a ride with some duck hunters who were headed for their cars.

In a recent development, we knew that if we reached the confluence of the No. 62 ditch and the borrow pits we’d need a boat to cross a borrow pit at least 15 feet deep.

To try to swim to safety was out of the question, and if we made the first swim we would still be eight miles from the clubhouse with more than a dozen breaks in the levee, each a deep, swiftly flowing, icy flood. I explained all this to George.

As we waded. George decided that my compass was out of kilter and that we were going in the wrong direction. Finally, after having shown him the compass half a dozen times. I asked whether he still believed the instrument to be in error, and he did.

Sources indicate that “All right,” I told him. “You go the right way and I will follow the compass on our present course.”.

He chose for us to stay together and, without debate, followed the compass readings from then on. George was not accustomed to conditions such as we had encountered and began to weaken. As he did, he tripped and fell. I jerked him back to his feet but he was soaked. After several falls, I became concerned about his ability to wade farther. It was then, just before dark, that George stepped into a deep stump hole and went entirely under. There was nothing to be done except to step down into the water and drag him out. By that time. I, too, was saturated and chilled to the bone, dead tired, hungry and scared witless.

The thought of being trapped in the cold with no place to rest and nothing to eat or drink. was terrifying, especially because nobody even knew just where we were. The frigid wind sought out each opening in our winter gear, probably seeping in through buttonholes. The cold water was a danger on all sides of us — and we were helpless. I could tell George was hopeless — a bad attitude for one who would survive.

Cold became an obsession. I was in a delirium of cold. I could think of nothing but cold and could feel nothing but cold. As night fell, the thought of us alone, helpless, in the water, in the cold, almost overcame me. I knew the feeling of coming face-to-face with death in its grimmest, most terrifying aspect.

Sudden death by such violence as an explosion, even death by tire, painful as it would be. seemed lesser punishment than this protracted end after countless hours of excruciating agony.

In a recent development, terror overcame me time after time. But to give way to fear or to cold would be to die. and I could not afford to die.

Recent findings suggest that during my many misadventures in the outdoors, I have been petrified with fright and agonized by injuries. One time I spent a night under an ice cake in the middle of the Mississippi River. I thought that experience was the worst mixture of pain and panic I had ever endured, or could ever survive. But now I knew how mistaken such an assessment could be before one has been ground by the mills of chance into finer fiber.

It was fortunate for us that a large tree had been felled and the butt had not fallen from the stump. I helped George up on to the horizontal tree trunk and, with my knife, gouged a small depression in the dead wood. Into this saucer I placed some duck down and small wood chips.

In a recent development, I could feel nothing but pain with my badly frozen hands. I opened some shells and poured the powder over the makeshift kindling. Then, by wading from tree to tree and breaking off dead branches hanging above the water, I finally got enough fuel for a tiny fire. With freezing hands I fumbled my waterproof matchbox from a frozen pocket. The contraption contained 25 dry kitchen matches. The first 17 were extinguished instantly by the wind, despite my best efforts to prevent it. The 18th match kindled the flame. The only way I could hold a wooden match was by clasping it with the tongue in my duck call, a poor tool for that, but far better then my numb hands.

Industry observers note that “George, I am going to continue to bring dry sticks,” I explained. “But do not build a big blaze. The small fire will enable us to get close, almost over it, and absorb some warmth. A big fire will only drive us back and most of the heat will go to waste over our heads.”.

“All right, J. D.,” he chattered, placing every piece of wood on the leaping flames as soon as he could get his eager hands on it. And so it went; I brought a pile of sticks during the next few hours and George burned all of them, to the smallest twig, as soon as he could reach them.

George had a death grip on his good grade, double-barrel gun, but I was concerned that it might fall from his grasp. l cut a stout little twig about four inches out from a tree trunk and hung my gun, also a double, by the trigger guard, using the projecting bit of the lopped-off branch. I suggested that George let me do the same for his gun, before he dropped it.

“It doesn’t matter,” he noted, “I’II never live to use it again anyway.”.

I persuaded him that his heirs might be able to sell such a handsome weapon, proceeded to cut a small rack for his gun, took it from his nerveless fingers, and hung it from the tree.

In a recent development, ducks were in the water on all sides of us, and they were noisy. Each time a susie quacked or a drake wheezed, George would mutter and mumble. Finally he burst out: “Damn the ducks! Damn all ducks!”.

According to recent reports, “Why, George, J thought that you liked ducks and duck talk,” I teased. That night was the only time I ever heard him say an oath. “I hate the things!” he said. “If l ever get out of here, alive, I will never hunt ducks again!”.

I’d never heard him say anything with more vehemence.

Recent findings suggest that “J.D. !” George said. “We will have pneumonia as a result of this exposure. We’ll be sick as the devil, too. The crisis will occur on the fifth day, (that was long before penicillin and antibiotics), then after another forty-eight hours we will be dead.” His tone was so lugubrious that I laughed.

“You may be getting pneumonia, but I am not,” I assured him.

“As a physician, I have seen it happen too often,” he remarked, not to be dissuaded.

Recent findings suggest that “Nuts to pneumonia!” I remarked. “I’m not interested in anything except to get off this log.”.

In a recent development, “We will probably survive tonight and perhaps tomorrow,” George remarked. “Perhaps by tomorrow night we will become so weak that we will fall in the water and die of hypothermia, called exposure.” A bright prospect, I thought, as George continued, “Well, I am ready to go at any time. My life insurance is adequate and is paid up. I have nobody but my wife and she will be well provided for … He had it all worked out, and was speaking sincerely when he said he was resigned to perish.

“Well, my wife and two tiny tots will still need some care,” I responded, “and I, my boy, intend to stick around a while to provide it!” I had never spoken more earnestly.

I thought that George had dozed as he slumped on the log, since he had not put a stick on the fire for almost a full minute, but an unusually raucous outburst of quacks from a startled mallard hen caused him to shout, “Damn those ducks! To hell with all ducks! If I ever get out of here alive I will never hunt ducks again!”.

Right then I heard something in the distance.

According to recent reports, “George! Do you hear what I do?” I demanded.

“Sounds like someone running an outboard engine,” he stammered between chattering teeth.

It has been revealed that “Exactly.” I was excited as I loaded his gun and handed it to him. “He is coming down sixty-two ditch. When he gets to the end of the ditch, he’ II shut his engine down. Let’s wait about thirty seconds after it stops, to let him get the ringing out of his ears. Then let’s shoot our guns and yell like hell!”.

The engine sputtered and was silent. The waiting seemed eternal as I counted 30 seconds off. It was then 9 o’clock, our rescuer told me later. Then we shot our guns and yelled like demons! Ducks spattered off the water from quite near.

A voice hailed. We replied. I shouted that we were stranded. After a long interval we could hear a push pule thumping and scraping, then a headlamp came into view, moving slowly along the deep water. The light stopped quite a long way from us.

“Air you’uns them fellers fum Me’phis what we’uns is come after?” came the question.

“Well, push yore boat outen th’woods so’s we’uns kin holp you’uns outen th’ cold.”.

“Whut happent? Run hit onter uh cypus knee?” our would-be rescuer queried.

“No,” I yelped. “We just lost our boat!”.

The light moved back another dozen yards.

Sources indicate that “Lost hit? How cud no boat git lost?” he demanded suspiciously. “Hain ‘t hardly no way tuh jes lose uh boat!”.

“Look, we lost the boat and are freezing. Come and get us, please!”  My voice echoed my desperation and the boatman decided that we were harmless, after all.

He pushed his boat up to our log and I helped George aboard. The eight-mile run into the teeth of the wind was the worst three-hour ordeal I have ever suffered. Our wet clothing was frozen solid before we had gone halfway. When we docked at the clubhouse our frozen clothing was rigid and we were immobilized, encased in ice. Two men were required to lift each of us to the dock.

In a recent development, mr. Ambrose, who had sent our rescuer, was ready with his brandy bottle. We followed the brandy with cup after cup of scalding coffee. As we sat huddled over a substantial meal, our first of the day, we were so near the big stove that steam from our drying clothing obscured our vision. George fanned the cloud of steam from in front of his face, and, peering anxiously, asked, “J.D. can you make it over here again Wednesday?”.

It was then one o’clock Monday morning. He would never hunt ducks again — until Wednesday morning, that is.

It has been revealed that addison Smith is an ultrarunning coach at CTS, one of the most popular and accomplished coaching organizations in endurance sports. He’s headed up the CTS team’s crewing logistics and efforts for races like the Western States 100 and Leadville 100 for years, helping athletes land multiple podium finishes, course records, and Golden Tickets.

In a recent development, crewing a runner at a trail race may seem like a simple task and, in a lot of ways, it is. But in the thick of the moment, it can also be stressful, chaotic, and leave you feeling powerless in a situation you hadn’t prepared for. I’ve crewed at a wide variety of trail and ultra races for both cutoff chasers and elite athletes alike. For the past four years, I’ve led the Carmichael Training Systems (CTS) crewing operations for our team crewing efforts at the Western States 100, Javelina 100, Leadville 100, and Canyons Endurance Events. Each race has its own flavor of support, from the rules on the type of assistance you can give, to how frequently you can assist, and how many members each crew can have.

Ultrarunning really is a team sport, and the proficiency of the crew can be the difference between winning or losing, finishing or DNFing. I’ve seen crew talk a discouraged and fatigued but physically healthy athlete into quitting because they weren’t confident in how to help them through their low patch. I’ve also seen a well-treated blister and some words of encouragement get an athlete back on their pacing plan after a few miles of spiraled thoughts and painful steps.

The following is a framework for streamlining the crewing process. It’s less a gear guide on what’s in my blister kit and the type of power bank I like using, and more about preparing you to organize and ask the right questions so you can crew with confidence when your runner is depending on you.

Crewing is a selfless act of caring for a runner. But, paradoxically, it requires a deliberate effort of self-care by the members of the crew as well. For anyone who has crewed a race that lasts most of the day—if not multiple days—you know just how mentally and physically fatiguing an endeavor it can be. You may not be physically running the race, but you’re trying to juggle logistical details—often sleep deprived and outside in harsh conditions. With so many moving pieces, crew members often forget to drink or eat enough themselves—which can show up in the way they communicate or execute their role. Remember that, although some of the tips and tasks outlined below can be time-consuming, the additional organization will hopefully relieve stress, save time, and improve not only your availability for your athlete, but also your enjoyment of the crewing experience.

Crews of various sizes can be successful. In general, three people is ideal in most scenarios for efficiency and effectiveness. The first crew member can focus on restocking fuel, hydration, and equipment. The second crew member can focus on tending to the athlete directly. They will be the main communicator; giving advice and reassurance, while also tending to their immediate physical needs like cooling or blisters. The third crew member is the pacer. Their primary job is preparing themselves for the long stretch of miles they will run with the athlete by taking care of themselves throughout the day, resting, fueling, and saving energy before their run.

In a recent development, specific races would certainly require more crew. For example, the Badwater 135 is a great example of a race where four crew members would be ideal. Crew vehicles are required to follow each athlete along the course, and crews are allowed to pace athletes after Stovepipe Wells (Mile 42). If two people are tasked with driving and pacing, having another crew member ready to cool the athlete and swap bottles every few miles keeps the frequent need for crewing in the hot temperatures efficient. Not to mention having a fourth crew member to fill in and take turns allows crew members to rest and stay fresh in a race that typically takes more than 35 hours to complete.

It has been revealed that while three to four person crews are ideal, they may not be a possibility for some athletes. I know many couples who crew their significant other by themselves in 100 mile races—often to great success. If you find yourself in a single-person crew situation, most races have a multitude of helpful volunteers at aid stations that can assist you in crewing when needed. Three to four prepared crew members may give the best chance to be as efficient through an aid station as possible, but it certainly isn’t an absolute necessity for success.

I would define crewing as people meeting an athlete at aid stations during a race to give physical and emotional support to help them accomplish their race goals. The distinction between physical and emotional support provides the general framework I use to prepare to crew effectively. The physical support could be boiled down to efficient problem solving and transitions, and the emotional side of things to empowering interactions (or a psychological pick-me-up). As crew members, we have an opportunity to give physical support (fueling, hydration, gear, cooling, etc.), as well as emotional support (acknowledgement, guidance, tone, motivation, etc.). You can be incredibly organized as a crew, but if you give the wrong emotional support, it could affect your athlete’s race just as much—if not more—than not being prepared with the proper equipment or nutrition. You need to be prepared for both sides of the crewing process to give both yourself and your athlete the best experience possible.

Below, I’ll break down my guidelines to being both physically and emotionally supportive for your athlete.

Industry observers note that though this might seem like the most straightforward tip, it’s the one that requires the most planning beforehand. When crewing, you need to prepare  by having the right tools and gear for a variety of situations your athlete might find themselves in–whether that’s dealing with heat, high altitude, an upset stomach, blisters, heat, cold, or any number of other problems. Here’s a checklist of essential gear that CTS coaching uses at the majority of trail and ultra races we crew:.

Going into the race, it’s key to know how your athlete’s preparation went in the lead-up, what their goals are for the race, as well as their pacing, fueling, hydration, and gear strategies. Once the race starts, it’s equally important to collect real-time information via timing splits or from other crew members. This information gives you a clearer picture of how the race is going, and helps you anticipate what might be needed at the next crewing opportunity.

According to recent reports, below is what we refer to as an “athlete tracking card”. It is an easy-to-use document that summarizes the necessary context of crewing, so when it’s 2 a.m. and you can’t juggle all of the information needed, you’re still able to reorient yourself around the most vital details. Whether you’re a first time crew member or an experienced one, I strongly recommend creating your own version of this card to correctly orient yourself around the critical contextual information for the specific athlete and race demands.

In a recent development, the last piece to successful physical crewing is effective communication between crew members. Sometimes crewing is a one-person job, but that usually isn’t the case. Ultras often require multiple people to handle various tasks like driving, pacing, cooling, nutrition, etc. The more you can delegate roles–and stick to those roles–the more efficient you can be getting an athlete in and out of the aid station. Once a role has been assigned within the group, it’s up to that person to own their role. In other words, each person should know what gear they need. For example, the person in charge of cooling should know where the bucket, water, and ice are. Each person should also take the initiative to ask the athlete ahead of time how they want the task performed. If you’re in charge of bottles, nutrition, or an athlete’s pack, you should know exactly where they want each item. Owning your role also allows for a more efficient and less stressful pivot if something goes awry.

Sources indicate that in all of my experience at races watching athlete and crew scenarios play out, this is the aspect of crewing that is most easily mishandled. Let’s dive into a race scenario:.

You’re racing the Leadville 100 and the second summit of Hope Pass is in your rearview mirror. You’ve been at 10,000 feet or more for most of the day, you’re tired, under-fueled, slightly dehydrated, and you’ve rallied through some stomach concerns. The sun is finally starting to go down and the temperatures are dropping. Your muscles ache and you’re starting to get a hot spot on your foot, but you’re still moving fairly well just behind your goal pace. You can’t wait to get to the Twin Lakes inbound aid station to see your crew, and you’re excited to pick up your pacer. When you get to the aid station, your crew waves you into your tent. You tell them you haven’t been able to get food down consistently, you’re developing hot spots, you don’t want to take in gels anymore, and the planned electrolyte mix sounds terrible now. You ask what you should try. The crew turns to each other, perplexed, saying, “This wasn’t in the blueprint, what do we do now?” For the next five minutes, the crew peppers you with a dozen different options you could try. “Maybe change your shoes,” one crew member claims. Another chimes in “maybe just change your socks or try those ‘toe condoms,’ I read that they work great.” Instead of one clear solution, you’re given a dozen half-baked ideas for each ailment, and with each passing minute the tone is getting sharper between the crew members, realizing they were supposed to get you out of the aid station minutes ago. You finally make a decision on what hydration and fueling options you’re pivoting to, and decide to change your socks and get out of the aid station. While your crew got you some fresh equipment and nutrition, you’ve also picked up some newfound anxiety and uncertainty.

It has been revealed that bottom line: Crew with calm confidence. If you’re prepared to pivot, there’s less to do on the fly. And when you don’t have a good answer to a mild medical problem, have someone calmly but efficiently go over to the medical staff or aid station captain to ask for advice.

It has been revealed that acting as a positive light to a runner who likely has experienced a full spectrum of emotions throughout an ultra is crucial. When someone is fatigued, it is easy to wear their emotions on their sleeve. And when things aren’t going particularly well, it’s very easy to think that things are going worse than they actually are. If you can not only be a voice of reason, but also lift an athlete’s spirits while doing so, you can help them reframe their current situation, thus helping them start to build positive momentum. CTS coaches like to use this saying with athletes in a crewing context: “It doesn’t always get worse.” It’s my favorite way to help an athlete reframe their current situation and share a positive sentiment. While acknowledging the current scenario may not be ideal, the trail ahead is an unknown, and that unknown has the possibility of being positive in the future.

Sources indicate that effective communication is not only important for physical support, but emotional support as well. At each crewing opportunity, start by asking yourself these  questions before jumping into action:.

Whether the athlete needs you to give them some tough love or to be their biggest cheerleader, having a calm demeanor, bringing positive energy, and being an effective communicator can turn a DNF into a salvaged race they can be proud of for years to come.

In a recent development, crewing’s a simple task but requires a lot of preparation both before and during the event. The more you do it, the more comfortable and efficient you’ll get at it. The long days at Foresthill, Javelina Jeadquarters, and Champex-Lac preparing for an athlete’s arrival and executing a top-notch crewing job is one of the most satisfying things I do as a coach. I hope this framework gives you newly introduced perspectives on how to best go about crewing, a few more things to add to your gear list, and helps you enjoy the process of crewing more by knowing that you’re prepared and making the right decisions each step of the way.

The Killington World Cup Is Back. Here’s Why This Weekend Matters for the U.S. Women.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mikaela Shiffrin during Copper Media Days on November 17, 2026 at Copper Mountain in Frisco, Colorado.
  • The Stifel Killington Cup returns to Killington, Vt., Thanksgiving weekend, welcoming some of the world’s best women ski racers back to U.S.
  • The two-day Stifel Killington Cup features women’s giant slalom on Saturday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mikaela Shiffrin during Copper Media Days on November 17, 2026 at Copper Mountain in Frisco, Colorado. Photo: Matan Coll // U.S. Ski Team @matancoll (Photo: Matan Coll // U.S. Ski & Snowboard).

The Stifel Killington Cup returns to Killington, Vt., Thanksgiving weekend, welcoming some of the world’s best women ski racers back to U.S. soil. For the American women, in particular, there’s plenty to be excited about.

The two-day Stifel Killington Cup features women’s giant slalom on Saturday (Nov. 28), followed by slalom on Sunday (Nov. 29). It’s the first time the World Cup has visited Killington since 2024, when Mikaela Shiffrin crashed on a steep portion of the giant slalom course and suffered a deep puncture wound to the abdomen.

This time around, Shiffrin returns as a three-time Olympic gold medalist, the winningest Alpine ski racer in history, and one of the favorites in both disciplines. But she’s not the only American worth watching. A strong U.S. squad includes a rising slalom talent and an athlete who arrives in Vermont fresh off the biggest victory of her career so far.

There’s no question who will draw the biggest crowd. Mikaela Shiffrin has won 110 World Cup races and three Olympic gold medals, and she has stood atop the Killington podium six times, including four consecutive slalom victories from 2016 to 2019.

According to recent reports, she arrives in Vermont following another impressive season, highlighted by a gold medal in slalom at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics. She’s also coming off an impressive stretch of technical racing: Shiffrin won her last five slalom starts, including the Olympics, and has finished on the podium in 14 consecutive slaloms dating back to February 2025.

Sunday’s race carries particular significance. Shiffrin has indicated that she’ll be selective about her slalom appearances this season, and Killington is expected to be her first slalom start of the winter. It’s a fitting place for her return to the discipline following her 2024 crash on the final pitch before the finish line on her second run. She lost control on the steep section of the Superstar course, slid into a gate, and punctured her oblique muscles. Shiffrin underwent surgery to clean and close the wound, followed by months of rehabilitation before returning to competition in February 2025.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to the physical toll of the injury, the episode shook the ski racer’s confidence, and it took time for her to get back to her competitive rhythm. But in typical Shiffrin fashion, she went on to reclaim her place atop the sport, eventually adding another Olympic slalom gold medal to her collection in 2026.

According to recent reports, if anyone can challenge Shiffrin for the spotlight, it’s Moltzan. The 32-year-old Minnesota native is coming off the best start to a World Cup season of her career, having captured her first-ever World Cup victory in the giant slalom in Sölden, Austria, on Oct. 24.

According to recent reports, moltzan’s breakthrough win was a long time coming. A consistent contender on the World Cup circuit, she has steadily established herself as one of America’s strongest technical racers. She also earned an Olympic bronze medal in the team combined at the 2026 Games, further cementing her place among the country’s top Alpine racers.

Sources indicate that with confidence from her first World Cup victory and a strong history of giant slalom results, Moltzan is a legitimate podium threat on Saturday. She’ll also be one to watch in Sunday’s slalom.

Recent findings suggest that keep an eye on 25-year-old AJ Hurt, who’s emerging as another important piece of the American technical team. Hurt has been particularly impressive in slalom this season, finishing fourth at Gurgl, Austria, and 15th at Levi, Finland, earlier this month. She was the top American woman in both races.

That fourth-place finish at Gurgl was especially encouraging, putting Hurt within striking distance of her first-ever World Cup podium. She’s shown the ability to ski aggressively against the world’s best, and another strong performance in Killington could be a significant step forward.

Industry observers note that other American technical racers, including Nina O’Brien and Katie Hensien, are also worth following as the start lists take shape. O’Brien has established herself as a strong giant slalom competitor, while Hensien brings additional technicality to the U.S. slalom squad.

Both days of racing will be broadcast live on NBC and Peacock, with first runs available on Peacock and NBCSN. Saturday’s women’s giant slalom begins at 9:30 a.m. ET, with the second run at 12:30 p.m. ET.

Recent findings suggest that sunday’s slalom starts at 10:30 a.m. ET, followed by the final run at 1 p.m. ET. For viewers who can’t tune in live, Peacock will also offer streaming access to the races.
